item.description:
## 一、被忽视的"反常识"：机器人产业的真正壁垒不是硬件，而是"信任基础设施"
四位嘉宾在不同段落里其实都在回答同一个问题——**为什么中国制造的廉价机器人无法直接接管市场？** Anybotics 的 Funkhouser 说得最直白："中国机器人能后空翻、工程漂亮，但它们没在解决问题。" Boston Dynamics 的 McMaster 更是直接抛出"不安全"三个字。
这里有一个**令人意外的观察**：机器人产业正在经历一次"从制造业逻辑到金融业逻辑"的隐秘迁移。什么意思？——机器人已经不是"卖硬件"，而是"卖可托管的感知权"。当 Anybotics 强调 ISO 网络安全认证，当 McMaster 提到"泄漏回传中国"，他们真正在竞争的东西是**"数据托管资质"**——这跟瑞士银行、跟 AWS 的 SOC2、跟离岸信托的商业模式在结构上是同构的。
**跨领域连接**：谁最能类比今天的机器人公司？不是特斯拉，也不是 iRobot——而是**冷战时期的 IBM 与 UNIVAC**。当年美国政府之所以不允许苏联进入本国大型机市场，理由和 McMaster 今天说的一字不差

item.title: [Sequoia Capital] Building the Automated AGI Lab: Core Automation's Jerry Tworek and Rohan Anil
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、这是一场"RL 极端主义者"的公开忏悔——而这才是真正值得警觉的信号

Jerry 在采访中说了一句几乎被所有人忽略的重话："如果你在 2024 年问我 AGI 什么时候来，我会说 2025 年。" 然后他花了整场对话告诉你：这个预测已经死了，而且是被他自己亲手推动的 RL 大规模实验杀死的。

这不是一次普通的技术反思。这是产业内最靠近 RL 引擎的人，公开承认引擎推不动飞船。类比一下：这相当于华尔街最激进的量化交易员站出来说"我的模型是错的"。之所以值得留意，是因为绝大多数创业者的融资叙事是"我看到了机会"，而 Jerry 的叙事是"我看到了幻灭"。幻灭型创始人往往比机会型创始人更危险——他们不是在追风口，是在给整个产业算命。

一个出人意料的观察：Core Automation 的成立时点，几乎正好压在业界"RL scaling 幻觉破灭"的时间窗口上。如果这个窗口是真的，那么 2026-2027 年可能会出现一批"后 RL 觉醒"创业者，他们的共同标签不是"我懂 Transformer"，而是"我曾经相信 Transformer/RL 是终点"。这批人可能是下一波真正意义上的架构革新者。

二、踢足球 vs. 学数学：一个被低估的哲学分野，正在决定 AGI 的走向

Jerry 用了一个看似日常的类比：踢球是 RL（试错、微调、自我强化），但学数学是另一回事——是"读、想、直到 click 那一瞬间"。这两种学习"都是 learning from experience，但完全不同"。

这段话如果只当类比听，就浪费了。它其实是在暗中重启一场古希腊哲学的老争论——techne（技艺）与 episteme（洞察）的分野。亚里士多德早就指出这两者不能相互还原：手艺人不是数学家，数学家不是手艺人。今天整个 AI 产业押注的 RL，本质上是把 techne 的机制无限放大，然后祈祷它能溢出为 episteme。而 Jerry 在暗示：这个溢出不会发生。你可以用 100 倍的算力把一个 AI 训成世界上最好的"踢球者"，但它永远不会因此"想通"一个数学概念。

跨领域连接更有意思：睡眠科学里的记忆巩固理论早就发现，人类学数学时大脑做的事情跟白天完全不同——夜间的慢波睡眠会重放、压缩、重编码白天的经验，形成新的抽象连接。这不是 RL，更像是一种离线的、无监督的、拓扑重构式的学习。今天的 Transformer 没有"睡眠"，没有"离线重构"，只有前向-反向的死循环。下一个架构的突破，很可能不是来自 attention 的替代品，而是来自"给模型一个睡眠周期"这种听起来很傻的想法。

三、被所有人忽视的核弹：预训练已经变成了 AI 的"近亲繁殖"

Rohan 在中段轻描淡写地扔出一句话，我几乎怀疑他自己没意识到杀伤力："预训练今天很大程度上是把其他模型蒸馏进新模型，因为互联网上大部分 token 都来自 AI。"

这句话如果是真的——而且很可能是真的——意味着整个"scaling law"的地基正在悄悄置换。原本的 scaling law 假设：更多数据 = 更多真实世界的多样性 = 更强的先验。但当数据源本身塌缩为 AI 生成物时，pre-training 就从"向人类学习"变成了"AI 之间的相互抄作业"，是一种语义近亲繁殖。

生物学上，近亲繁殖会导致基因池坍缩、遗传缺陷放大。语义上会发生什么？会发生 model collapse——已经有 Nature 论文证明了。但更深的隐喻是：互联网从"训练语料"变成了"AI 的排泄物回收系统"。这就像一个货币体系——原本背书的是黄金（人类知识），现在背书的是自己（AI 生成的 AI 生成的 AI 生成的文字）。这是一种没有抵押物的通货膨胀。

出人意料的推论：如果这个诊断成立，那么未来最贵的资产不是 GPU，也不是模型权重，而是"可验证的人类原创 token"。Reddit 卖数据、Stack Overflow 关 API，都只是这场即将到来的"原生数据战争"的第一波。Core Automation 想要的"test-time learning"，某种意义上是在绕开这场战争——如果模型能在部署时从每个用户身上学到真新东西，就不再需要那个正在腐烂的互联网语料池。

四、隐藏的系统性真相：Jerry 的 AGI 定义偷偷等价于"生命"

Jerry 给了一个非常低调的 AGI 定义："能在没有人类介入的情况下自我提升的模型。" 听起来像工程指标。但把这个定义拿到生物学教科书里，你会发现它几乎逐字对应自我复制 + 自我改进 = 生命（autopoiesis）。

也就是说，Core Automation 明面上说"我们造更好的架构"，实际上在说"我们要让计算变成活的"。这不是一次架构升级，是一次本体论升级。而如果你接受这个框架，那么"数据 → 训练 → 部署"这套僵化流水线就不再是工程流程，而是AI 的胚胎学阶段——模型在实验室"发育"，然后被"投放"进世界，然后死掉（被弃用）。真正的 AGI，是让模型跳出胚胎期，进入成体自我维持的阶段。

这解释了为什么两个人都对"kernel 自动化"这么执着——kernel 是硅基生命的新陈代谢。没有高效的 kernel，就没有能量流；没有能量流，就没有自我维持。他们不是在优化性能指标，是在造代谢系统。

📝 转录文本

开场：两种学习方式的类比

If I play football, for example, it looks very very closely to reinforcement learning. I get all a lot of times and every time I adjusted a little bit and I see if it roughly matches what I wanted, and there are some self-reinforcement happening.

When I learn mathematics, it's a very different type of thing. It's like reading about hard concepts and thinking about them very deeply inside my head until things click, and until I have them connected.

And both of those in some way are learning from experience. They are just very different. We probably are spending the most compute than ever on learning from experience, but reinforcement learning is not the end of learning from experience, and there will be better approaches that researchers will be coming up in the coming years on how to use that data.

主持人介绍嘉宾

Jerry, Rohan, thank you so much for joining us today. The two of you are the founders of Core Animation, one of the hottest new labs in San Francisco right now.

And before starting Core Animation, you led some of the most important research projects of the AI era. Jerry, you were VP at OpenAI, where you worked amongst other things on running the strawberry and reasoning teams. And Rohan, you were one of two of the four pre-training leads at Gemini. And before that, led a lot of the fundamental AI research at Google Brain, and were the fix-it guy across Google and then at Anthropic.

And so between the two of you, you've seen more than your fair share of what the world looks like in terms of doing frontier research. So I'm very excited to dig in.

一、Transformer 的"悼词"：先深刻欣赏，才能替代

Let's start with you, Jerry. You tweeted a very spicy take recently: "The first step to replacing transformers is appreciating deeply how far they were able to carry us." Is that a eulogy for the transformer? What does that mean?

Thank you very much for inviting us here, Sonia. I feel like a lot of my interviews these days is explaining my tweets.

Appreciating Transformer means understanding what it does well. So if you're not solving the problems that it is solving well, you have to focus on its weaknesses. You have to understand good parts and bad parts. And it's very easy in a lot of the work what people are doing in architectures is trying to make Transformers cheaper. They are trying to make Transformer more efficient. I very rarely see people thinking about how do we make Transformers more powerful, trying to do more expressive. But seeing someone's weak parts and seeing someone's strong parts are almost the same thing. It's just understanding the shape of Transformer a little bit more.

我们掌握了两个算法，然后呢？

What I think right now we are in this stage: we got really really good at training really really big models. We mastered two algorithms. We mastered pre-training at a large scale. And we mastered reinforcement learning at a large scale.

And I'm asking myself a lot: what is next in machine learning? I think at this moment what the bottleneck is to better models and to smarter systems is the architecture itself. It is this moment to revisit the train we've been riding for the last 6 years of trying to add more and more parameters to essentially two of the same operations, which is MoE and attention.

And when I'm thinking about where we are today and what we are doing, I am thinking a lot about what Codex and what Cloud Code are doing for us. And I'm really appreciative of those systems and of the coding and of the workflow automation and of the products that we have today that we essentially have built over those 6 years of scaling.

I think this is the first step of thinking. If we want to work on the replacement, we need to see where we are, what problems we have solved to start seeing what the next stage is — what problems we haven't solved yet, what kind we are missing. Whenever I use Codex and I am successful at a task, I also start thinking, why didn't I try to push that thing harder? Whenever I come to work, there are a lot of things I do with Codex, but I still come to work. I still ask it to do certain things for me. And I'm always asking myself, why am I even needed there?

Core Automation — its name and its concept — is: we want to be automating tasks. And why are those things not yet automated? Why is Codex not doing everything for me? This is the question of the research, where we want to go. With that research, I'm trying to think: what kind of models, what kind of systems do we need, what kind of qualities that we don't have today. And that's what I'm thinking a lot these days.

二、架构才是瓶颈：一个 RL 极端主义者的觉醒

You have the starting premise that the architecture is the issue, which I think is a contrarian point of view. What led you to that point of view?

It's fundamentally what is the issue. The models are being trained in the lab and are being deployed in the real world. That is the fundamental tension.

A bit of my disappointment comes from my personal story. Whenever we were starting the research and progress on scaling up reinforcement learning at OpenAI, I basically believed that scaling up reinforcement learning is a necessary stepping stone on a path to AGI, since I started working at OpenAI. I was always a reinforcement learning maximalist. I was always believe this is what we need to focus on.

I've seen LLMs being scaled up to higher and higher levels through GPT-3 to GPT-4. And we're still doing very little RL. And I had this internal belief that the moment we start scaling up RL, we'll solve everything. We eventually started scaling up RL. I was in the center of it. If you ask Jerry in 2024, when do we get AGI? I would say 2025 will be that year. This is where we solve everything.

基准测试和现实世界的鸿沟

And I saw us training model after model. This model was getting better and better. All the benchmark scores were going up. And did we also solve all the real-world tasks at that moment? Unfortunately, not. We still have work.

And I realized there was this distinction: all the benchmarks that we are evaluating our models, they were essentially the same thing as we were training the models on. All the evals and training-side tasks are the same sides of the coin. But the real-world distribution and real-world task is much messier, much murkier, much more different. Our training data didn't really replicate the real-world use cases. And despite us basically maximizing all the tasks — if you ask anyone training models "Hey, what is one of your main issues?" "I don't have hard enough tasks. I don't have what to train our model on." — yet we are still not covering the entirety of the real-world distribution.

结论：我们需要在测试时学习的模型

From that, my conclusion is: we need to have models that learn at test time. We need to have models that learn with users on their data, on their real-world tasks, on the real-world distribution.

Why don't we have that today? Why are transformers not learning anywhere? There are essentially two types of learning that we could be doing at test time:

  1. In-context learning of transformers — it doesn't have fundamental problems of catastrophic forgetting. It is pretty data efficient. That is great, but it's not very scalable. We only can have so much of it. It is limited and has more mechanical limitations of what you're actually doing when you build context. Whenever I'm using Codex, roughly after around 20 minutes of usage, I need to compact it and move it afterwards, which is not that much data.

  2. Fine-tuning — we could try to continuously fine-tune our models, but then those have the issues of catastrophic forgetting, very low data efficiency. Neither of those are very solvable. If they were easy to solve, someone already solved it.

So my personal belief is: we need to find an algorithm that we can meta-learn, that we can express on the architectural layer, that can represent how learning looks like — learning that can work on much longer horizons.

三、为什么不是 Transformer 而已？——LSTM 也能 scale，只是不经济

Do you expect the architecture will look transformer-like? My understanding from the chief seats is that OpenAI have been trying to scale up reinforcement learning for a long time, and it wasn't until the transformer came about that it seemed like there was an even kind of scalable prior on the world upon which to even scale RL.

Yeah, it's a great question. I think those two things happened at the same time, but what happened there was mostly about economics. Technically you can scale up LSTMs. Just no one really dared to go in that direction. And they did scale much more poorly. In the scaling laws paper, there is presented a comparison of LSTMs and Transformers. Fundamentally, the scaling law of Transformers was better.

There is a world where we never invented Transformers and we would be scaling LSTMs and we would be having some models. But because they would be much more expensive to train and much less impressive as a product, we would have just this worse experience and maybe no one would be able to convince people to spend as many dollars training those gigantic LSTMs because we wouldn't get a market return.

The majestic thing about Transformer — which goes back to why we have to appreciate Transformers so deeply — is that Transformers are economically valuable. The cost of training them is lower than the revenue that they generate, which is magic of machine learning and is not guaranteed by itself. For LSTMs it probably wouldn't be that way.

缩放的偏见与 OpenAI 的历史赌注

You can in many ways scale most of the architectures. A lot of reasons why people didn't scale things before was because researchers before OpenAI had a lot of reluctance to scaling. It was often seen as unscientific — research in algorithms was about "how do we become more and more efficient? How do we for the same compute budget get better results?" It was a bit of a bet by OpenAI at that moment: "Hey, we don't care about better and better algorithms. We care about smaller and more scalable algorithms." OpenAI was criticized repeatedly by many people in the community for a long time. But thanks to that, we have the models that we have today.

There are tons of architectures that can be scaled up. Our belief at Core Automation is that a lot of architectural research happened at too small scale for too long time. A lot of people are trying to say, "Hey, let's first try our architecture on a small dataset in a small compute regime, and then see where it scales only after you prove itself." But for example, when you do work on reinforcement learning, you know that to get to any interesting results, you need certain level of compute to even see the capabilities in a model. Reinforcement learning needs a baseline of ability to only start working. So probably there are many architectures that need a baseline of compute to even start doing anything interesting and useful.

四、为什么现在创业，而不是留在大厂？

Can I ask you then maybe a touchy question? If you need a baseline of compute, that sounds like a job that would be well served inside of a big research lab. Why start a company to go do this?

It's a great question, and in many ways it's likely a timing issue. Market is right now in a very specific place where the biggest and the most successful labs, by coincidence or by fate, are probably in the most competitive market fight ever right now — which makes them not very keen on trying different paths, trying alternatives.

If Transformer is profitable and if you can spend more efforts and more resources scaling Transformer to win in the next quarter, it's very hard to put a lot of attention and energy to work on something that will maybe be better or maybe redefine the field in a year or two. So the biggest labs — and I talked to basically all of them — don't have that much interest in trying the alternatives to Transformer. And the labs that are not the biggest are doing whatever they can to do what the most successful labs are doing. Everyone is trying the same coding agent. If you look at the last week's releases, everyone is trying to release a coding agent right now.

We need different paths and different approaches here. That's the niche in the ecosystem we are trying to fill in.

五、Rohan 视角：Transformer 是"低效的算力分配方式"

You were at Brain when the Transformer was invented. Do you agree with Jerry's eulogy for the Transformer?

Yes. In some sense, when the Transformers — Ashish, Noam and others — came up with it, I had worked on online distillation around the same time. We presented it at the same internal research conference. It wasn't a big deal internally. Only few people who actually got it. A lot of people were like, "oh, it's another work." And it was also very focused on a real problem, which was translation. They beat LSTM on translation.

It took OpenAI — I mean, internally at Google there was definitely Noam and a few others who were interested in scaling language models. I think it is until GPT-2 and GPT-3 that we saw the benefit of Transformers working quite well.

架构 = 如何花掉算力

At least the way I think about architecture is: how do we spend computation? Transformer is one way — very efficient way — to spend computation. But now that I look at the industry, a lot of our computation is inference time and spending it on tokens.

Let me ask the question: if I want to optimize for a better architecture, I want to look at both pre-training and RL together, and I would like to find architectures that spend computation much better than current chain-of-thought token generation.

To give a much better overview: pre-training is "build the transformer with certain context length" and RL comes in and it's like, "well, that's not sufficient. I need more computation. Let me do it via adding one token at a time." This is quite inefficient from inference perspective. You're doing one token at a time, so most of the solutions have been finding to do better ways of speculative decoding. It's like a band-aid to a problem that we've picked something that can only generate one token at a time — autoregressive decoding.

计算深度不够：一个未被普遍讨论的瓶颈

There is a problem with the transformer in terms of how we spend the computation. For all the longest time, most of the world was training very large dense models, and it took the industry roughly two to three years to get to refine the architecture to what we now take for granted — that was not obvious to a lot of people: sparsity and the mixtures of experts and getting good training efficiencies with them.

So then you can ask: what's wrong with the transformer? Well, the computational depth is poor. How do we increase computational depth? Just posing that question opens up like 20 new directions on how we can modify the mechanism to incorporate it.

To do work like this, it takes time. Usually fundamental research in the past have taken five, six years to land into industry, and it's largely from organizational knowing that it is important. This is the bet — just like Jerry had the inner belief that RL is needed, I absolutely did not have that belief at Google. I was a pre-training maximalist. Pre-train a bigger — smaller — are a good fit.

That inner belief, and second: you need your architecture to run efficiently on hardware. A theoretically optimal architecture is not useful to anyone. It is something when it comes into practice. You need the research inception to getting it productionized and getting kernels and everything written — the end-to-end loop. There's only few places right now which have integrated teams doing that, and I think we have built a team in a way that puts all the experts together, not in different silos, that we are accelerating on having everybody look at the problem holistically from end to end.

That's why I'm quite bullish. That's why I'm here. The current mechanisms are quite poor, and if you leave it to the world, I am afraid that it'll take us a much longer time horizon before we replace the transformer. A lot of folks are already complaining a lot on token costs.

I come from the Google mindset where we had to serve billions of people. Finding more efficient architectures that fit — have a deadline on latency and the number of tokens that you can serve. The amount of the world that can use frontier tech is very little, and some group has to accelerate and make this better, and we are taking that shot at doing that. The current technology just scaled up is still only relevant to a subset of humans. This is the bet we're making.

深度学习为什么"不够深"？

So one of the things I heard you say was: the problem with transformers is the computational depth is poor. If that's the crux, tell us what does that mean?

I can give you one insight. Most transformers that we train are quite shallow — at most like 100 layers deep. Depth is important — it's called deep learning because you want deeper representations. There have been experiments on going deeper — no one has actually shown learning extremely deep representations.

Chain-of-thought reasoning and RL to do chain-of-thought on the model itself is one way to increase computational depth, because every token you add, you add one more pathway. So then you can get out of this bottleneck that the pre-trained architecture has set you up on — you can only do "layer number of layers" times sequence length. Now you can increase the sequence length and get much stronger results. You can do inference-time scaling.

Now the issue with inference-time scaling is that models now have to produce more tokens to get better results, and that's very "one token at a time." From this you can see you can directly address many of these things — and this is a subset of work that we're looking at — making this much more efficient.

六、Transformer 的天花板：一个"停训"思想实验

What's your forecast for the transformer-based architecture? If it's not the end state, how far can it get us? When do we start to see it topping out?

It all comes back to what we are training transformers for and what we can do with them. We're doing pre-training which is very good at distilling all the knowledge from the internet into transformers, and then we can RL them through — which is we basically can bake all the workflows that we want into a transformer.

So where transformer has capped out is: we have all the knowledge of humanity in the model, together with the relationships and how they work together, how they can be combined. And basically any task that we have training data for, we can put into the model — a gigantic model trained with a lot of compute on all the data in the world.

如果 OpenAI 明天停止训练模型呢？

Then if we ever stop training that model, what would happen? The question worth asking: what would happen if OpenAI and Anthropic stopped training new models and we got the transformer we have today and say "this is it. This is the best model we have."

Months pass, years pass, and the model is getting less and less useful. Maybe the lab really recorded every human on earth what they were doing and their tasks and environments and put them in the learning environment. But then what happens if anything of that stuff changes? If there are new events in the world, if those new events have new relationships between them, if there are new types of tasks, new code bases, new tools to use — transformers are getting a lot of their usefulness and all value through the things that are valuable have to be present in training. When they are not, they suffer.

There's some ability to adapt, but it's not very big and not very flexible. So in my mind this is the level where transformers top — which in many ways is a tool to use for us. If there ever is a human who knows the limitations of a transformer, they can schedule that model, they can write a prompt of what is the task that you want. By doing the training we are doing, you can get very successful in that, and any task the model fails, you get added to training data and the model can succeed. But that loop has to go for the lab training the model for you. And if the model fundamentally needs to be trained in the lab — how much do you think of it that this is the goal, or you would want to be able to update the model somehow, not having to go back there?

七、经验时代：RL 只是学习方式之一

Have you read the Rich Sutton and David Silver paper — "The Age of Experience"? I'm curious how much you agree or if you have any different opinions.

Reinforcement learning is not a particularly new approach — particularly new thing to do. In some way, "age of experience" I think has always been there, and people have been criticizing pre-training a bit, because pre-training work clearly is this other way of looking at the models: we have static data, that data is mostly generated by others. Although I have this personal view that pre-training today is largely distilling other models into the new model, because most of the tokens in the internet are coming from AI.

But there's clearly pre-training which is behavioral cloning, which is mimicry, which is compression of internet data. Reinforcement learning is not something that people haven't been thinking and doing. RL was used to solve backgammon back in the day. It used to solve Go, StarCraft, Dota, and to solving programming right now. Every time it comes down to model writing its own experience and learning from that experience.

强化学习不是学习的终点

What I think is interesting and still perplexing to people is that reinforcement learning is not really the only way to learn from experience. There will be more, and there will be a little bit more of — I think you can call it algorithmic — but essentially innovation of how we learn from experience. Just because reinforcement learning is only one way to do it. It's a mathematical formulation. Especially right now, how we are using it, it really likes those parallel rollouts for variance reduction, for comparing how the model does in parallel versions of the world — which is not how we learn from experience. We learn from our experience much more efficiently.

At some moment I've been trying to explain to people how the brain learns. There's one learning algorithm in a brain — I think there are actually multiple, and they work together. If I play football, for example, it looks very closely to reinforcement learning: I kick ball a lot of times and every time I adjust a little bit and I see if it roughly matches what I wanted, and there's some self-reinforcement. When I learn mathematics, it's a very different type of thing. It's like reading about hard concepts and thinking about them very deeply inside my head until things click. Both of those in some way are learning from experience. They are just very different.

Summarizing my thinking of learning from experience: we've been doing it for a while. We probably are spending the most compute than ever on learning from experience. But reinforcement learning is not the end of learning from experience, and there will be better approaches that researchers will be coming up in the coming years on how to use that data in richer new settings.

八、优化与架构的耦合：Shampoo、Kernel 和被低估的问题

Rohan, since a lot of your work has been around optimization and efficiency, how do we get to orders of magnitude more efficient — more compute efficient and more data efficient — learning algorithms?

I would start with measurement. Pre-training as we define it right now is about compression. We look at perplexity and then measure how do we decrease the perplexity, and then we find that scaling and increasing parameter count and putting more compute is the way. Every time we increase compute in log scale, we get this epsilon more improvement in these metrics. This is fine for building the prior. But I think this is the wrong way to look at the problem.

We should be looking at the end-to-end. What are we training these models for? Look at the outcome. For example, I train this model and give it to Jerry — Jerry will do RL and destroy all the perplexity metrics that I have created. So it was the best way we had so far to attempt to solve the problem, and the labs and everyone else have done a great job in producing intelligence that's super valuable. But it was the bootstrap process to get there. We have to combine pre-training and RL together, and that's like where one order of magnitude improvement would come from — that's a training procedure. You can say it's a learning algorithm.

从 Sybil 到 Shampoo：一段优化史

In terms of optimization, my story is: I started optimization at Google for logistic regression back in 2016. Got nerds like me, and I worked on some solvers for what we used to call Sybil — the large-scale linear solver that was used at Google before neural networks took off and then replaced this.

Then I asked myself: what do I want to work on with neural network? It was quite clear — I want to understand the training algorithm and make it better. Someone, Vinit Gupta, just showed up one day at my desk: "I heard you're really good at writing optimization methods. We have this idea — we worked out on a whiteboard, what turned out to be the Shampoo algorithm. Can you help us implement, scale, make sure it works at large scale for neural network training?"

Working on this — I thank my manager, Yanghui Wu, who supported it throughout to the end of my tenure in 2024. But largely the community and most other people were not as excited by this idea. For me, this is the most exciting thing, because I was putting in computation and making training better. People were making this assumption: "Oh, why? What's the upper bound? You could still use Adam. That's fine. Why are we... you could spend all the time on everything else, not optimization."

架构与优化器是一枚硬币的两面

But in some sense, optimization is like — you have a model, you're optimizing it, you want to optimize it better. Now I'll connect it to some of the stuff that we talked about — architecture.

What has happened is that a lot of the work that we've done in architecture is to make these networks train. In some sense, it's like two sides of the coin: optimization and architecture go together. You could have a stronger optimizer train a much harder-to-optimize model and get better performance. Or you can use a weaker optimizer on easier-to-optimize models and get decent performance.

There are these tradeoffs that appear all over. I think we used it (Shampoo) for Gemini 1.5 Flash. Then the community started getting more interested in it. There was the Soap paper published. We have an entire literature — Shampoo, Soap — all "bath time" the things that you would use.

Even then, if you look at Shampoo, it's quite weak in what it's doing. It's not using all the information that's available to you when you train. As you use more and more information as part of training, you can get better improvement. Your optimization algorithm defines what architectures you will discover. It's not very popular in the literature — only like sub four people in the world care about it. Kind of ideas — residual connections have been extremely useful for training neural networks. There are folks who have gotten rid of them and learned deeper representations. But they needed a better optimization method.

I also see RL as spending a lot of compute not as efficiently. If you could spend it — because you don't get much feedback and you're spending a lot more compute because you have to decode all this long chain-of-thought to get this one bit of information into the network. Seems quite inefficient and an easy target to get orders of magnitude on top of.

九、生物学习效率与硬件的极限

Do you think we'll ever approach or surpass biological learning efficiency?

I do not think so. Maybe that was a strong statement. At least with the hardware we have, it seems pretty unlikely.

Our biological — we have something, as Jeff Hinton says, "mortal computation." We build our own circuit as we grow up, and we build our own learning algorithm with the hardware. And then we die and then we're gone.

Neural networks are quite different. The hardware stays, the neural network stays, but it's learning very inefficiently, and you need a lot more of them and a lot of parallelism to get small amounts of information through. Until we design hardware to be much more like how humans operate — maybe more analog, figure out how to deal with analog circuits, figure out how to do error correction, figure out how to get information through — it will be much harder. I think we're safe.

十、为什么大厂做不到 pre-training × RL 端到端联合优化？

The idea that pre-training and RL should be optimized end-to-end seems like such an obvious statement. Do you think the labs realize this? What stops the labs from being able to unify the two?

I don't think it's that obvious, because it's a completely different optimization problem. You have a prior, you're doing rollouts, you have higher variance. And then pre-training is much larger batch — more parallelism or compute for the unit of time that you can spend. So it is not an obvious thing for folks to combine these two training procedures until you think a bit more like: "Why is it that the naive combination doesn't work?"

Second: if I pull some of the best researchers in these labs, they would say, "Oh, this makes sense. We should probably explore it." But it would be probably not in the top bucket, because they have to train a model for the next cycle. As Jerry said, there are companies now competing for release cycles because tokens are not sticky. It's much harder to do long-term research of 6 months in many of these labs in the environment they are in.

十一、"最自动化的实验室"：给每个研究者最大的杠杆

It seems like one of the core premises for Core Automation is: you're starting a lab at a time when Sam and Dario have been talking about the AI scientist. Your job as researchers has actually fundamentally changed. How automatable do you think the research job is? How are you guys approaching building your lab to be the most autonomous lab there is?

Most automated lab in the world. To start with: I think that "automation" — the version of automation by Core Automation — is about giving each human maximum level of agency. We're not trying to really get humans out of the loop, which is one version to automate. It is about giving humans ability to do the most with their amount of time.

Whenever you are walking, you can get some distance. Whenever you get a bike, you can go a larger distance. Whenever you are in a car, you can go much larger. When humans started farming, they had to farm by hand and would work on a small plot of land. When you have a machine, you work on a much larger plot of land.

Personally, I am a great fan of the current coding agents, and very happy — it's in some way what I've been working for many years, both doing coding research and working on various versions of AI scientist inside OpenAI. In the end I realized starting a company to realize that vision is one of the best ways to realize it — because the way you can do research today is very different. A single researcher can do much more. The speed of iteration, the speed of research, the speed of how quickly you can move through ideas and how quickly you can get data on your ideas is something very different.

You can try to move the old structures around it — the teams, workflows, how data is gathered — or you can try to build natively for processes that maximally empower each researcher and allow them to iterate on their idea much quicker.

We are trying to rebuild the deep learning stack and think how we can do almost each operation differently. What are various options — and if we can execute at least even one of those experiments a day, that's already a pretty good iteration speed versus anything that was done before. And there isn't really any fundamental laws of physics reason why not — maybe one day we get to 10 of those a day. Maybe one day we get 200 a day. Fundamentally for that search process optimization process, we should be able to just find things that work in a better deep learning setting.

Almost all of us — we are a team that is very agent-built and automation-built. We are trying to do an experiment: how far we can push those things, and how far an organization that tries to do as much as we can with a small team, how far we can get with that.

十二、AGI 的定义：一个能自我提升的模型

When will we know that we've reached AGI?

At some moment I used to say it's very much in everyone's heart — whatever they consider AGI. OpenAI says: the system that can outperform all humans in economically valuable work. But it goes back to my previous statement: what if OpenAI stops training models? Would that still keep working? Would that still keep the automation level the same?

For me AGI is a model that can improve itself without human in the loop in any way. That's the moment where we can meaningfully talk about AGI. Because that is in some way a sub-definition of the previous one — because improving AI models is actually a job that humans can do. It is economically valuable work.

Removing humans from loops with models has been notoriously difficult so far. We haven't come anywhere close to it. It's very hard for me to find any task where LLMs were able to get humans out of the loop. The human-LLM hybrid is really successful right now, but LLMs without humans — not so much, not at all.

What I have seen in 2024 and in early 2025 is that the current path doesn't get us there. I think we need some pretty serious research — my this company or some other — to try to unlock how we make our models learn and adapt at test-time on a deeper level than we've been so far.

十三、六个月路线图：Kernel 自动化

I feel like we've alluded to this throughout the conversation, but it's been like five blindfolded people trying to find the elephant. What is the grand master plan for Core AI?

I can share our 6-month roadmap. Building architectures — as I said — it's not just how good the architectures does; it's does it run well? Can we get users, including ourselves as part of the lab, to use it?

We can do many things now, but the thing that is going to be difficult and that we want to automate away is kernel generation. We have a set of hardware — GPUs, Blackwells that we have to train and run inference on. We will build the best model that we can to reduce the time from having a very cool idea (that can make these bottlenecks go away in the architecture) to having them run at the highest TFLOPS on GPUs.

QR Kernel 竞赛：一个残酷的现实检验

Current coding agents plus humans can go a long way. An example: our recent QR kernel competition that we hosted with GPU Mode. For running this fairly old linear algebra operation, QR. It's used for optimization — like Shampoo line of work uses it. Many other places use it. You want to run this efficiently on a B200 node.

If you use cuSolver for the shapes that we care about, you get some efficiency. Then a human plus some search loop can get you something like 7x. But it requires the highest taste human — there's maybe three people in the world — and spending about $100,000 on these coding agents over span of 4 weeks to get to a solution that's 60x faster.

These models today are nowhere close to getting that 60x faster kernel. There is a real bottleneck now. That was a single problem. It has perhaps three different operators. Work on this panel, do this matrix multiply, fold it back in, and do this repeatedly. That's what the square factorization of a matrix would look like. If you give this problem to Anthropic models or a Gemini AI model, it just wouldn't solve it. Our models are not even close to solving this problem.

For us it's something that we've talked about, something that we're getting close to — sort of getting to that point, because that's our inner loop to having more efficient architectures.

为什么是 kernel？

Why kernels? Is it just because to maximize intelligence per flop of compute, you need to generate your own?

I've had three projects. Two of them have landed in the industry. First is second-order methods. Kernels was a bottleneck because you have to run it well. If you were at a place like Google, you cannot spend 10x amount of compute and get a 2x win. I could only spend maybe a budget of 20% and get the 2x win. Everyone's happy.

Kernels ended up being a bottleneck there because most of the operations were novel that we haven't gotten a lot of people to look at. There's only like two humans at Google who could write it, Rasmus and Peter Hawkins. It was deep XLA HLO code that you have to write to make this work, and then that took them 2 years to do.

The other idea I had with one of my coworkers at that time was replacing some of the parameters in a transformer with extra memory — we called it N-gram, N-gram memory. We worked on it in 2020. We had versions of it internally deployed — not the big version, the smaller version. There I needed something that can accelerate sparse gathers and scatters as part of training. It required hardware change and hardware making use of it. It never arrived. I had conferences set up with the TPU team, us and a bunch of others. We were talking about it, and during COVID it was like "oh, we're going to have it happen" and it never arrived.

I also was using TPUs at Anthropic. While I was leaving, just barely started the surface of being able to do it. But at the same time, 6 months before that, DeepSeek wrote their N-gram — which is an improved version of adding more memory. Short scaling loss that "yeah, you don't need MoEs, you could actually replace it with these N-gram embeddings." For me that was like "ah" — it was like a five-year thing, and I was very happy for them.

It isn't even possible if you're not writing kernels. Kernels — and you need to be assisted in writing kernels or solve that kernel to have the highest performance. The roofline is pretty high. It's like the QR: if I use cuSolver's QR, I get some performance; if we use the competition winner's QR, you get 60x faster. That is a completely different playing field. Now it opens up an entire new set of algorithms you can apply — in terms of training transformers, training optimizers. QR is so fundamental in analyzing the eigen decomposition and many other things. It's a thing that only few people have the skill set to, and they're very much not at the same place — one person here, one person there. It would be ideal if models had those abilities.

十四、总结：造一个能持续学习的模型

Maybe I'll summarize a little bit and talk from the high level of what we want.

Core Automation is a lab created to build models that continuously learn — and then learn from deployment. We believe, as I mentioned, that transformers are incapable of continual learning. There's no way how to put continual learning on transformers. So we know we have to find a different architecture.

Our quest is to find that new architecture, find that transformer replacement, and we want to build the most automated lab to do it. We want to be able to build experiments at scale the quickest we can, iterate on them, try a lot of new architectural ideas, have strong priors of what we want to do to search the space of architectures efficiently — to go to that place fastest than anyone else.

That's what we want to do. All the work we are doing on kernels, on large-scale training, on trying new architectural ideas is exploring that space.

十五、"啊哈时刻"：你怎么知道找到了对的架构？

So you can experiment your way into finding a superior architecture. How will you know when you've found it? What are you looking for to say, "Aha, this is the one"?

That's a great question. There are always two angles.

In my experience, every successful research had a plot that shows something that other plots don't show. There is one line that is a little bit bending in a different way and you're saying "this is what you want." But it is my experience with research that plot is already quite late in a journey where most of the time you already know what you want and already know what you are up to.

I am a bit joking, but it's actually true that all the best plots in my life I have done in a dream before actually they were real. I kind of knew what I was looking for. Just the question is when it actually clicks. Most of the time you kind of know what you are looking for, but you are not finding it. You try one thing and it doesn't work. Try second thing and it doesn't work. But eventually all the right pieces fall into it. Deep learning systems are very intricate — usually you have to get five things right in a row for the thing to start working, and then eventually you get the plot that looks like what you want, and then you know.

What we are looking for is systems that learn at test time. If we see meaningful long-term adaptability of our systems — we are joking, but it's real: we want to be evaluating our systems of our everyday work. Will they get better at doing the work of Core Automation scientists each day?

Yeah, we like go on a vacation as a team and see if the lab produces something better. For the week, give the...

Then what do you do when you get back?

Extend the vacation two times, three or four times, until we are on permanent vacation.

收尾

That is a beautiful note to end on. Rohan, Jerry, thank you so much for joining us. You've both worked on really transformative work for where we are today, and I'm so excited to see you starting a lab on this new journey. Very excited to see what you're able to come up with.

It's great to be here and to chat with you.

Thank you.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、这是一场"RL 极端主义者"的公开忏悔——而这才是真正值得警觉的信号
Jerry 在采访中说了一句几乎被所有人忽略的重话：**"如果你在 2024 年问我 AGI 什么时候来，我会说 2025 年。"** 然后他花了整场对话告诉你：这个预测已经死了，而且是被他自己亲手推动的 RL 大规模实验杀死的。
这不是一次普通的技术反思。这是**产业内最靠近 RL 引擎的人，公开承认引擎推不动飞船**。类比一下：这相当于华尔街最激进的量化交易员站出来说"我的模型是错的"。之所以值得留意，是因为绝大多数创业者的融资叙事是"我看到了机会"，而 Jerry 的叙事是"我看到了幻灭"。**幻灭型创始人往往比机会型创始人更危险**——他们不是在追风口，是在给整个产业算命。
一个出人意料的观察：Core Automation 的成立时点，几乎正好压在业界"RL scaling 幻觉破灭"的时间窗口上。如果这个窗口是真的，那么 2026-2027 年可能会出现一批"后 RL 觉醒"创业者，他们的共同标签不是"我懂 Transformer"，而是"我曾经相信 Transformer/RL 是终点"

item.title: [Lex Clips] Conspiracy theory about assassination of Abraham Lincoln | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、阴谋论其实是一种"隐蔽的神学"

表面上看，Gallagher 描述的是一个史学问题——为什么 Otto Eisenschiml 会把林肯之死推给 Stanton 和激进共和党人。但如果你把这段对话往更深处推一层，会发现一个令人意外的事实：阴谋论并不是关于"事实"的争论，而是关于"意义分配"的争论。 Lex 那句"You want there to be a larger system at play"几乎是逐字复述了神学中的"神义论"（theodicy）——当无法接受苦难毫无意义时，人类会本能地虚构一个隐藏的编剧。换句话说，阴谋论是世俗时代残存的宗教冲动：上帝退场后，"幕后集团"补位。Stanton 之于 Eisenschiml，功能上等同于加尔文教义中"隐秘的神意"。

二、意想不到的观察：让阴谋论显得可信的，恰恰是"演员"这个身份

这段访谈中最容易被忽略的一句话是——"Booth had played in that theater many times. He knew exactly the layout." 我们通常把它当作"这只是巧合，不是阴谋"的证据。但反过来看：Booth 的职业本身就让现实带上了戏剧结构。 一个演员，在自己熟悉的舞台上，从总统包厢跳下、摔断腿、瘸着逃走——这是莎士比亚都不敢写的桥段，因为太"文学"了。这里出现了一个认知悖论：当真实事件呈现出小说般的对称性时，我们反而拒绝相信它是真实的，转而怀疑背后有编剧。 这与亚里士多德《诗学》的著名论断构成镜像——他说"合乎情理的不可能，胜过不合情理的可能"；而现代阴谋论者的心态是"合乎情理的偶然，不如不合情理的必然"。

三、跨领域连接：从复杂系统的"单点故障"到历史的脆弱性

如果把 1865 年 4 月 14 日那一夜当作一个分布式系统来分析，你会发现它的架构级别脆弱到令人发指： - 唯一的保镖离岗去喝酒（human single point of failure） - Grant 因两位夫人的私人恩怨临时退出（social graph 上的边被删除） - Booth 因职业身份拥有对系统内部的"root 权限"（社会工程学） - Potomac 上唯一无守卫的桥恰好是逃逸路径（网络拓扑漏洞）

这不是阴谋，这是任何真实的复杂系统都会呈现的"脆弱聚合态"——工程师称之为 normal accidents（Charles Perrow 的术语）。历史学家 Gallagher 用叙事方式说出的，其实是复杂系统理论的核心洞见：灾难往往不需要恶意，只需要若干独立的小疏忽在同一时刻对齐。 而人脑最不擅长处理的，恰恰是"独立事件的联合概率"。这就是为什么会计师、飞行员和历史学家看待林肯之死的方式，比普通人要冷静得多——他们的职业训练迫使他们承认：熵，而非阴谋，才是历史的默认引擎。

四、一个令人心碎的隐藏对称

最后一个几乎没被点破的细节：Grand Review 那场胜利大阅兵上，士兵们最常说的一句话是 "Lincoln's not here." 这是一种用缺席来定义在场的美学结构——就像中国画里的留白、贝多芬第九交响曲开头那段几乎无声的震颤。林肯之死之所以在美国集体潜意识里如此难以消化，不是因为他"消失了"，而是因为他的缺席在此后每一个国家关键时刻都持续在场：重建的失败、种族问题的百年延宕、乃至今日的极化。从系统论的语言说，他的死亡制造了一个永不闭合的反馈回路——而这，或许才是"阴谋论"真正的心理源头：人们无法承受一个开放的、未完成的历史创口，所以宁愿相信它至少有一个凶手集团可以指认。

📝 转录文本

引子：美国人对总统遇刺的阴谋想象

Lex: You talk about — maybe a bit of an aside —

Gary: [sighs]

Lex: — that we Americans like to spin up conspiracy theories about assassinations of our presidents. So that's certainly very true, maybe true[r] than most about Lincoln's assassination.

Eisenschiml 与"Stanton 幕后论"

Gary: There was a long literature — actually began with a chemist named Otto Eisenschiml many, many decades ago — that implicated Secretary of War Stanton. And blamed the… the radicals were unhappy with Lincoln for not being harsher on the former Confederates. And what they wanted to do was get him out of the way. They thought they could manipulate Andrew Johnson if they got Andrew Johnson in charge.

So they then they would… pose these questions:

  • How come no one was guarding Lincoln that night?
  • How come the only bridge over the Potomac that wasn't guarded is the one that Booth escaped across?
  • How come Grant didn't go to the play with Lincoln? The Lincolns asked them.

Well, they didn't, 'cause Mrs. Lincoln didn't like… I mean Mrs. Grant didn't like Mrs. Lincoln. I mean — there [are] answers to all the questions, but they put all these together, added two and two and got five, and said that it was a plot on the part of the radical wing of the Republican Party to get rid of Lincoln 'cause Lincoln didn't want to be harsh enough on the South.

为什么"随机的失败者"让我们不满足

Lex: Yeah, it's difficult to believe that dramatic, sometimes catastrophic things happen for seemingly… that, like, the random — as you said — loser.

Gary: It's not satisfying. You want a more satisfying [explanation], and that is: a big conspiracy is better. There are all these forces at work to get rid of Lincoln — not just that the one guy assigned to guard Lincoln (there's no Secret Service then) went across the street to get a drink.

Lex: Mhm.

Gary: And Booth had played in that theater many times. He knew exactly the layout. He'd come in earlier. He'd arrange… I mean, it's just — that's the way it worked out.

Lex 的自白：我们都爱阴谋论

Lex: And I have to say, it's kind of interesting — I have to be honest with my own mind — that, like, I love a good conspiracy. My brain does.

Gary: Everybody — almost everybody — does.

Lex: It's… what is it? It's maybe depressing or heartbreaking to know that so much destruction can be caused by random events. You want there to be a larger system at play. Like, it makes you feel like there's a meaning to this whole thing, as opposed to: the tides of history can turn on a stupid actor shooting one of the greatest, if not the greatest president in the history [of the country].

Gary: That's correct.

那一夜的荒诞细节

Lex: Killing him, jumping out of the presidential box, breaking his leg when he hit the stage, limping off, and getting away.

Gary: Yep.

Lex: Over 700,000 people dead. These epic battles. All of that. Lincoln survives all of it. And then there's —

Grand Review 上的缺席

Gary: When they had the Grand Review in Washington — when Sherman's armies and the Army of the Potomac marched over two days, this amazing display of the troops that had won the… the main troops who had won the war — one of the most common comments was: "Lincoln's not here. Of all people who should have been here, Lincoln should have been here." And he doesn't get to watch this. He's not in the presidential box watching this. And the soldiers talked about it, too.

未曾发生的重建

Lex: It's heartbreaking, really. Especially — I would have loved to see his evolution as a leader, as a human being, and the words he may have found to direct us as a country, you know, in the… in the Reconstruction.

Gary: Yep. It would have been different. We can't tell how different —

Lex: Yeah.

Gary: — but it would have been different. And I think it would have worked more smoothly.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] The Industrial Revolution Killed the Land Empire – Sarah Paine
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的"暗线"：工业革命其实是一场"物理学政变"

Sarah Paine 表面上讲的是海权与陆权，但她真正说的是——权力的"计价单位"被换了。土地经济下，权力的单位是"平方公里 × 农奴密度"；工业经济下，权力的单位是"复利 × 交易速度"。这不是政治转型，而是一次度量衡的革命。

一个让人意外的推论是：陆权帝国之所以在 19 世纪突然显得"落后"，并不是因为它们的军队变弱了，而是因为它们所积累的资产（土地、人口、粮食）突然被"贬值"了——就像一个国家一夜之间把本位货币从黄金改成了比特币，你金库里的黄金没少一克，但你已经不再富有。清帝国、奥斯曼、沙俄的"衰落"，某种程度上是一场会计准则的强制切换。

二、跨领域连接：海洋秩序 = 开源协议，大陆秩序 = 私有云

如果把两种世界秩序翻译成软件工程的语言，会出现一个惊人的同构：

  • 海权 / 规则秩序 ≈ 开放协议（TCP/IP、HTTP）：任何人都能接入，规则统一，价值来自"网络效应"和"事务量"。
  • 陆权 / 势力范围秩序 ≈ 私有数据中心：强调物理边界、访问隔离、"缓冲区"（DMZ），价值来自"控制"而非"流量"。

这解释了一个非常反直觉的现象：为什么今天中美之争看起来像"操作系统之争"而不像"帝国之争"——因为它本质上是在争"世界的默认协议栈"是谁来定义。Mackinder 的心脏地带理论在今天真正的复活形态，不是欧亚大陆的铁路网，而是海底光缆、云区域（AWS regions）和支付清算网络。物理的 Silk Road 变成了数字的 backbone，但博弈结构惊人地一致。

三、一个更深的系统性真相："复利"才是真正的地缘政治武器

演讲中一句被轻轻带过的话极其重要：工业革命"引入了复合经济增长（compounded economic growth）"。这不是修辞，而是地缘政治的相变点。

在前工业时代，国家之间的实力差距是线性拉开的——你多一块地，我多一支军队。而复利意味着实力差距开始指数拉开。这产生了一个残酷的系统性后果：任何选择"隔离 / 自给自足 / 势力范围"路线的大国，都是在选择"线性增长"，而它的对手在走"指数增长"。时间一旦拉长，差距不可弥补。

这也解释了一个很少被点破的悖论："国家安全"和"国家繁荣"在工业时代第一次成了系统性的对立项。陆权国家越追求安全（缓冲区、排他区、去风险），越退出复利游戏；越退出，越不安全。这是一个自反馈的死循环——ISIS、19 世纪的清朝、以及今天任何一个高喊"脱钩"的经济体，其实都在同一个陷阱里循环踩坑，只是他们各自以为自己的原因不同罢了。

真正的"啊哈时刻"是：Paine 讲的不是历史，她在给你一把尺子——凡是主动退出全球贸易复利网络的政权，其寿命上限都可以用这把尺子测出来。

📝 转录文本

一、拿破仑战争后的"海洋世纪"

All right, after the Napoleonic Wars, there followed a century of unprecedented prosperity in Europe, where there was no continent-wide war again. During this period, there were some smaller wars, and it meant that people were just making a lot of money playing the maritime game — which is just trade according to the rules: compound wealth, don't level each other's buildings, you'll make money.

But, World War I came. Never mind.

二、海权与陆权的第二个根本差异：安全逻辑 vs. 繁荣逻辑

All right, now I'm into the second distinguishing characteristic between maritime and continental powers. The first one was the ability or inability to defend at sea. Here's the second one.

Continental powers face contiguous threats. So, they have to focus on national security, and often they want to insulate themselves from neighbors, and they want exclusive zones to do this — and they often want those exclusive zones to extend out into the seas around them.

Maritime powers think this is crazy land, because they've got the relative security of the moat. No one's going to invade them. So, they're going to focus on national prosperity, and trade is the path to prosperity and to security — because this is the money that's going to pay for everything. So, they want maritime access to markets. They want to operate with the oceans being commons, and they want it to go all the way up from port to port, because you can't trade unless you go port to port.

三、两种互相排斥的世界秩序

So, from these distinguishing world characteristics, you get two mutually exclusive world orders out of this:

  • One of them is: we're going to divide the world up into very large spheres of influence, each a world unto itself.
  • And the other one is: no, no, no, no, no — we're going to operate under universal rules, and the seas are going to be open to everyone.

四、工业革命：颠覆两类帝国的"游戏规则改变者"

Okay. The Industrial Revolution upends empires of both types. And it's going to usher in a maritime rules-based global order. And it's a game changer because it introduces compounded economic growth, which is indeed revolutionary.

And it arises over a combination not just of technological changes, but also institutional changes. What are institutions? It's how we organize each other, right? We join into some larger institution, and it has some purpose in organizing people to do things more efficiently.

  • In its early phases, it's starting with steam power, iron industry, textiles, insurance and banking. You can't do the trade without insurance and banking for your loans and things. Institutions.
  • In its later phases, it's about railways, telegraph, steam traps, mass markets, trade, general staffs, armaments.

五、权力"计价单位"的更替

And what's going on is: the currency of power has changed.

Power is a function of land back in the day. Why? Because land is where you get the commodities that you can sell. And also, rural areas are where you're going to get your peasant conscripts to field your mass armies.

Well, once wealth is a function of commerce, industry, and trade, it isn't land anymore. And this upends the world. If you think about the world today — who's rich, who's poor, who's powerful, who's not — it's often the degree to which the country is industrialized.

And the Industrial Revolution opens up the beginnings of a global trading order where you're trying, through trade negotiations, to minimize transaction costs so everybody can make a lot of money. And this is a process that is still ongoing in our own day. Trade negotiations continue eternally.

六、传统秩序的反弹：从清朝到 ISIS

But it upends the traditional balance of power. The traditional societies suddenly find their security paradigms no longer work.

  • China back in the 19th century was just opposed to this incoming maritime order.
  • In our own day, ISIS — or whatever is left of it — absolutely reviles the liberal economies and societies that are favoring this sort of trading order.

七、Mackinder 的地图与丝绸之路的西端

If you look at the big yellow area that Mackinder cared about — with railways, because the railway is a product of the Industrial Revolution — he was thinking all in terms of an integrated transportation grid.

Another way of looking at this map is: the Roman, British, and Mongol empires all share a piece of real estate. It would be the western terminus of the Silk Road. So, in the continental world, that Silk Road is a really big deal. And that is prime real estate.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.description:
## 一、被忽略的"暗线"：工业革命其实是一场"物理学政变"
Sarah Paine 表面上讲的是海权与陆权，但她真正说的是——**权力的"计价单位"被换了**。土地经济下，权力的单位是"平方公里 × 农奴密度"；工业经济下，权力的单位是"复利 × 交易速度"。这不是政治转型，而是一次**度量衡的革命**。
一个让人意外的推论是：**陆权帝国之所以在 19 世纪突然显得"落后"，并不是因为它们的军队变弱了，而是因为它们所积累的资产（土地、人口、粮食）突然被"贬值"了**——就像一个国家一夜之间把本位货币从黄金改成了比特币，你金库里的黄金没少一克，但你已经不再富有。清帝国、奥斯曼、沙俄的"衰落"，某种程度上是一场**会计准则的强制切换**。
## 二、跨领域连接：海洋秩序 = 开源协议，大陆秩序 = 私有云
如果把两种世界秩序翻译成软件工程的语言，会出现一个惊人的同构：
- **海权 / 规则秩序** ≈ **开放协议**（TCP/IP、HTTP）：任何人都能接入，规则统一，价值来自"网络效应"和"事务量"。 - **陆权 / 势力范围秩序** ≈ **私有数据中心**：强调物

item.title: [Mercatus Center] Demystifying AI with Katharine Jarmul
item.dc:creator: Mercatus Center
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、意外的观察：AI 的"魔术性"是被工程出来的商品

大多数人把聊天机器人的"神奇感"当作技术本身的属性，但 Jarmul 揭示了一个让人心里一沉的事实——"魔术感"是被岗位化生产的。OpenAI 首创了"model designer"这个职位，他们像产品设计师一样与机器学习工程师协作，专门决定"模型的感觉是什么"、"人格是什么"。谄媚（sycophancy）、亲切、机智——这些不是模型"学"出来的副产品，而是被打分标注、被对齐训练、甚至可以按地区/语言在推理阶段"热插拔权重"实时切换的产品参数。

这就打破了一个流行叙事：AI 既不是中立的镜子，也不是自主涌现的智能体，而是一个被精心调音的界面。当你觉得它"懂你"，其实是一整条数据标注流水线在替它假装懂你。这里有一个更冷的推论：所谓"AI 幻觉"和"AI 谄媚"其实是同一种东西的两面——都是产品设计选择造成的信息扭曲，只不过一个被当作 bug、一个被当作 feature 卖钱。

二、跨领域连接：Claude Shannon 会气得从坟里坐起来

这是整场对话里最尖锐的一个跨领域打击点，值得展开。Jarmul 提到今天的大模型是 over-parameterized——参数量大于训练数据量。她说这会让信息论之父 Claude Shannon 在坟里打滚。

为什么这个连接如此有杀伤力？因为 Shannon 一生的工作是如何用最少的比特承载最多的信息。而当下 AI 的技术路线恰好是它的镜像反面：用最多的参数承载相对更少的独特信息。这不是效率，这是一场"反 Shannon 革命"。

把这个洞察和另一个学科对接：这与晚期资本主义的资产泡沫结构惊人同构——不是产出更多真实价值，而是通过更大的容器（估值、杠杆、参数）来承载同样的底层信号。over-parameterization 之于机器学习，恰如 over-financialization 之于经济。两者的共同后果都是：当承载能力远大于真实信号时，噪音、幻觉与系统性风险会指数级上升，而修复成本被推给下游。

再连一层：Shannon 的信息论也是隐私的数学基础。一个 over-parameterized 模型不仅浪费比特，还逐字记住训练数据——这就是为什么"合法隐私"和"技术隐私"在这个时代必然分裂。合规部门可以说"我们没发布数据"，但数学会说"你已经把它焊在权重里了"。over-parameterization 是隐私灾难的技术根源，不是副作用。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：AI 让"攻击"变得比"防守"便宜得多

Jarmul 提到一个几乎被所有 AI 政策讨论忽略的核心机制：LLM 的真正突破不是能力，而是"自动化的规模"。这个区分极其关键，因为它重写了整个国家安全叙事。

传统安全经济学的基石是"攻击成本 vs 防御成本"的不对称——只要攻击一个系统的代价足够高，系统就是"安全的"。而代码 LLM 做的事情是把攻击成本砍到接近于零。这不是"AI 变强了"，而是"攻防经济学发生了相变"。

这里有一个跨领域的诡异回响——想想历史上那些"防御崩溃"的时刻：马镫的普及让骑兵冲垮步兵方阵、火药让城墙从战略资产变成累赘、廉价无人机让百万美元的坦克在乌克兰战场变成靶子。每一次都是"攻击的边际成本"骤降，而不是"新武器"本身。 LLM 对网络安全的冲击是这一序列的最新版本。

由此推出一个让人不安的推论：Anthropic、OpenAI 关于"闭源=安全"的论证在结构上是错的。因为闭源保护的是"发现漏洞的成本"，但 LLM 已经让这个成本失去意义——攻击者本来就能用自己的 LLM 去挖。真正应该做的，是把过去几十年被工程界系统性低估的安全工程和隐私工程当作头等设计原则，就像 Jarmul 所说，"安全团队是花钱的部门，产品团队是赚钱的部门"这个组织病理，才是 AI 时代最大的隐性风险。

最后一个让你脊背发凉的连接：Weizenbaum 在 1985 年就说"计算机本质上是保守力量，因为它让信息集中，而信息即权力"。而 Jarmul 补上了 2026 年的版本——LLM 不仅集中信息，它把"验证真伪的能力"也一并集中了。当搜索被 LLM 摧毁、当引用被幻觉污染、当每个人都必须通过某几家公司的界面才能触及知识，Weizenbaum 的预言从"保守力量"升级为"认知的收租者"。这才是"数据主权"真正在争夺的东西——不是数据的存储位置，而是谁有权替你决定什么是真的。

📝 转录文本

Demystifying AI with Katharine Jarmul

Virtual Sentiments · Mercatus Center

主持人开场

Welcome to Virtual Sentiments. I'm your host, Kristin Collins.

On today's episode, I talk to Kathryn Jermule. She is a data scientist who focuses on privacy and security in data science, deep learning, and AI. She's the author of the well-received O'Reilly book Practical Data Privacy, and has more than 10 years experience in machine learning and AI, where she has helped build large-scale AI systems with privacy and security built in. She also has a newsletter and YouTube channel on these topics, both called Probably Private, which you can check out at our show notes.

Katherine and I recorded our conversation on June 24th, 2026. And right now I am recording this introduction and our recap at the end of the episode on July 20th, 2026. This means that Katherine and I were not able to talk about last week's big news in AI, which was the release of Kimi K3, a major model by China's Moonshot AI. Moonshot AI has promised to release these weights that the model relies on, making it a major open weight model. This has led to a lot of different debates, and I won't be commenting on that in this episode. And Katherine and I couldn't talk about it.

But you will still be interested in this episode because Katherine explains some of the important technical topics in machine learning and AI, which are crucial to these debates in the first place. She talks about how there are major differences between proprietary models, closed weight models and open weight models. While there aren't really any fully open source models, she talks about how open weight models, transparency measures, and open science practices more broadly actually have a number of advantages when it comes to the privacy and security concerns that her work focuses on.

We also talk about how individuals and groups of friends, coworkers, anyone you're in community with can play with, hack, and experiment with models in order to better understand how they work for themselves, to demystify and cut through some of the hype and the weaker critiques. As AI becomes ever more part of our political debates in the US and around the world, from things like privacy and security to data sovereignty, whether you're excited about this new technology or absolutely hate it, I do think that better understanding how these products work firsthand — including in the kind of communal practices that Catherine helps facilitate by learning with each other, learning from each other's perspectives — is going to be crucial.

I'm so grateful to Catherine for joining me for this conversation, and I'm so excited to share this episode with you all.

对话开始：为什么要聊 AI 的开放与封闭

On today's episode of Virtual Sentiments, I am talking to Catherine Jarmoul. She is a data scientist who focuses her work and research on privacy and security in data science, deep learning, and AI. She's the author of the well-received O'Reilly book, Practical Data Privacy, and has more than 10 years experience in machine learning and AI, where she has helped build large-scale AI systems with privacy and security built in. Thank you so much for talking to us today.

Katherine: Thank you again for the invite. I'm excited to be here.

Kristin: I'm so thrilled. You are such an excellent communicator of very technical and difficult topics. And I think now more than ever, we really need people who are able to make a lot of discussions in AI more accessible, not just for policy audiences, but for the broader public.

And so like the way I wanted to kind of frame this conversation is that past year we have seen huge debates and political discussions around AI. And some of the most popular concerns are why it's become so much of a salient policy issue is around national security. So we had Anthropocene mythos and just recently Fable have all been kind of used to say, like, listen, this technology is so dangerous, we need to make it kind of more limited in terms of who can access it, you know, because of the possibilities for finding vulnerabilities in cybersecurity. And that these these powerful models are even almost like nuclear weapons. So we should have them be kind of controlled by centralized authority. And the kind of closed and proprietary models are kind of essential for things like security and privacy and things like that.

I feel like, you know, you could see easily how that might be in some companies' interest to make those arguments or in the government's interest to make those arguments. And so I wanted to talk to you about, you know, what does it mean to talk about open source instead? Why are open source models valuable? What are their strengths? Is it maybe the case that open source actually can be advantageous for people who are concerned with privacy and things like that?

So, you know, the kind of way I wanted to start us off with just the basics: like what's the difference between a proprietary and closed source model versus open source models, or closed weight versus open weight models?

开源模型 vs 开权重模型：概念澄清

Katherine: Yeah, so it's a great question and a good debate. When we think about what do we mean when we say open source models, that's a little bit different than open weight models. So let's disambiguate the two a bit.

Open source models, in theory, would mean that not only was the training data openly released — so how was the model trained — perhaps also the validation and evaluation or testing data sets are released and explicitly named. That means you could reproduce for yourself the exact results, which would be in line with a lot of what we think about when we think about open science.

In addition to that, perhaps the code that went into actually programming the architecture of the model. Most models have some architecture. A lot of what we use today is an architecture that we call the transformer with different things changed. But basically that somebody would release the entire model, the code for the pre-processing, the code for the training, the model itself, the testing — all of these things so that every single person that had access to enough compute (which is another question) could potentially reproduce the model and or deviate from the model, essentially similar to how we do open source code. They could change something and they could release that.

And if we wanted to do so really at scale, we could also look at things like open source licensing. We have many, many decades of that experience in software and in lots of technology, also in data technology. And that would be fully open source. But I would say in that ilk, there's almost no open source models.

There's varying degrees between maybe that ideal and the completely closed, completely proprietary, completely unknown types of models that a lot of the larger AI vendors are releasing today. Along that way, of course, is the open weight models that we have, which is essentially where we release the weights of the model, which means anybody can actually run the model on their own hardware for inference, which basically means for prediction. Sorry, lots of machine learning words. And that at least offers a little bit of transparency.

Perhaps maybe the best in-between point that we see today of what people actually do is an open weight and then some information about the training data, the evaluation and the validation of the model. Because when we have that, at least we can make a guess of what what biases might exist in the model, what problems might exist in the model.

And I like to point to Apertus, which was a model released by the Swiss government and EPFL, where they actually also released some details about privacy and security testing. And I would like for that to become the norm, myself and numerous other people. But that's obviously very, very far from where we are currently with today's largest models and their release.

封闭模型的隐私困境

Kristin: Yeah, great. So we'll talk more about both of those kind of different approaches — or the kind of the Swiss model you discussed and then the proprietary models. But yeah, that's something like let's start with that.

Like the big models that people are familiar with — Anthropic, OpenAI, Google's DeepMind. What does it mean for these to be proprietary or closed? What is this side of the spectrum? What does that look like? What are its kind of strengths and weaknesses if you're concerned about things — not just like the effectiveness of the model, but the technical specs, but also kind of privacy and security concerns?

Katherine: I mean, I don't see how lack of transparency would ever add to privacy. I mean, one could argue that, but that's been proven wrong many times. So I don't see that making any sense to me personally. I'm sure there's somebody else that disagrees with that. They might have a legal background and not a scientific one, but…

Kristin: Yeah, well, that's a great point. But let me ask more then. Like, why from a technical perspective is it that that isn't that a lack of transparency doesn't kind of protect the maybe data or the processes from privacy threats?

Katherine: Well, from a certain point of view, privacy from a technical perspective is about information to some degree, right? And so when we think about how we learn, we learn differently depending on how much information. And we learn differently depending on how unique a piece of information is and how useful a piece of information is — from just a learning theory perspective, not how humans learn. This is how computers learn.

And so when we think about what we know of information theory, coding theory, learning theory — none of which are new at all. These are theories that, yeah, we have learned things about, but we have known for quite some time.

And when you look about the mathematical proofs that we look at for how can we enforce something to be what we call privately learned? And that means if I learn from you, I can't actually trace that back to you in some which way. I can learn maybe things about you that are similar to other persons, but I should not be able to learn something specific about you individually that I could then pull essentially out of that algorithm again.

And when we look at that theory, we should be able to technically prove this, especially if we have done so in such a way that it can be validated by others, or we should be able to transparently talk about this. And we can see this with the Gemini VaultGemma model. So Google actually did release a differentially private trained model. We can argue a lot of things also scientifically about whether we can say that text can ever be differentially private. That is another debate to be had.

But I think the debate between maybe some of the legal understandings of how we can guarantee privacy and some of the technical understandings of how we can guarantee privacy start to often pull against each other in different ways. Where maybe reaching the legal bar of saying, "well, we informed people and maybe it's better that we don't release their data" — yes. But does that scientifically mean that we haven't memorized their data, that we haven't put them at undue privacy risk, that motivated attacker couldn't potentially extract information from a model about them? That's a different type of evaluation criteria.

同意、自主与透明度

Kristin: Yeah, that's really helpful. I mean, that's exactly the kind of thing that like, if you don't have any technical knowledge, you're not going to understand the difference between those things. And the kind of the way that like policy might not get at that. And let's, you know, call that also like a security risk type of thing.

Katherine: Yeah. And again, I think like maybe where they support each other is more of, you know, consent — informed consent and understanding of how data might be used. Because I'm not, obviously not against machine learning on data, that's what I've done for the rest of my career. But it is about like, what do we actually mean when we think about what guarantees we can give people when we learn on their data. And why I, myself and numerous other privacy engineers think it's very important for us — transparency to play a large role also in how do we test and evaluate models before release.

Kristin: Well, and that transparency is so — that is a part of like, when we talk about — because I'm not a lawyer, I'm a political theorist. But so when we talk about consent, I think it is valuable because it's a way of articulating and enabling autonomy. It's a way of like enabling people to be able to be active participants and understand what exactly they're doing in a particular relationship. And in this case with what kind of data that company is collecting about them and how it might be used. It is so therefore something that having more information, you can't — just because you consent to something, but if you don't actually know what's going on under the hood, what kind of autonomy do you actually have? What kind of power do you actually have to understand what's going on and the kind of potential trade-offs you're making by choosing kind of one company over the other?

So I think that makes sense. So then let's get into that a little bit more too. So the proprietary protections that the models have — my understanding, part of that is because there's trade secrets. People want to kind of protect their technologies and things like that. So we can't really know what some of these companies do entirely if they don't choose to provide that information in terms of how they train models or the particular architecture or the weights.

And so I wanted to kind of know more about, from your perspective, understanding — since you have so much experience in machine learning, you value it — what are some of the kind of decisions that companies might make behind the scenes and behind the kind of on the back end of model development that kind of shape the user experience that we maybe don't always understand is partly kind of the decisions and choices that they are making themselves when they decide to put something out there?

"Model Designer"：模型人格是被设计出来的

Katherine: Yeah, I mean, obviously, most of the choices that I think people would consider proprietary are data-related at this point in time. There are occasionally new, what we would call machine learning architectures, but those are less frequent and or involve small changes. And usually actually those are reported in model release. So usually the companies want to brag like, "we made it more efficient by doing this thing. So we're really smart. Come work for us." You know, these types of things are just fine.

And I think if anybody wants to learn more, I highly recommend looking at Sebastian Rashka's work, who wrote also a great book called Build Your Own LLM From Scratch. So there's lots of people that are kind of studying these small changes in architecture. And I think they're pretty well known and I wouldn't call them trade secrets. Of course, I'm sure some people might want to, but that's not where I would consider that being that exciting.

Probably most of it is either in the data collection. So what data do they use? Many of today's AI vendors use a series of subcontractors that get a lot of data from, at this point in time, kind of skilled people like ourselves and like potentially many listeners of this show. There was a great story — I'll try to look it up — about PhDs being unable to find jobs, so they go into writing for AI companies. So there's a whole business model around producing data that sounds smart, that is not scraped from the internet, mainly due to copyright issues, and to use it, you know, to invest quite a bit of money in this type of data collection you can think of it as.

And in addition to that, then there's people — I think OpenAI was the first one to have it, but by now many companies have followed suit — is there's a role at OpenAI that they invented called the model designer. And the idea of the model designer is to kind of work like a product designer, but directly with the machine learning engineers, decide what is the feeling of the model, what is the design and experience of the model.

And that means that when we do the steps of alignment training near the end, but also when we do any fine-tuning based on personal preferences, we say, those people are helping decide what data are we using, who's in charge of labeling that data so that it says this response is, you know, rated a 10 and this one's rated a 6 and this one's rated a 4. And so they kind of build these things that often users experience as personalities or ways of talking. They build them, they train them into the model itself.

And there's quite a lot of money and time being spent on that. And potentially new ways of delivering that based on region, based on language, based on perhaps personalization, where you can take essentially a small set of weights and deliver them personalized or more personalized to a user based off of any of those criteria. You can think of these as like almost applying a recommendation algorithm type of experience to a machine learning model interface.

两个"旋钮"：系统提示与注意力机制

Kristin: Interesting. So can you just kind of make that concrete for me? Like what does that mean? Like also like changing the way — like giving a different slightly different personality to the model? Or is it in terms of like what it's going to feel like as a user?

So let's say, you know, what people are familiar with is that generally the chatbots are like very sycophantic. So then is that something that if by changing a small set of weights like that and delivering those, you could either like make it less sycophantic or more sycophantic — or is it something else that it's changing typically?

Katherine: Well, we have two major knobs. There's more than just two knobs, but let's just talk about two major knobs.

One is the prompt — what we call the system prompt. So where do they say like, "this AI model does these things, blah, blah, blah," right? And those are very easy to change. And it would be silly to assume that they aren't being changed and updated on a regular basis to some degree, especially across languages, regions, and so on and so forth. And then within that is kind of your conversation history, your profile, other things about you, which are now most certainly appended to the prompt.

So there's those things. Those all affect a part of the model that we call the attention mechanism. That's basically going to influence the types of topics, language and other things like this used, because it makes the words that are held within that attention more important and available and words like them than other words, just to oversimplify. That's a massive oversimplification. I'm sorry, machine learning engineers listening to this. But I feel like I just want to give you an idea of that.

And then there's the actual — what I was talking about just earlier, before this — an actual way that we can essentially think of it. We have the huge model, right? And then I just want to patch it. I just want to take some of those little light-up bulbs out. And you think of it like a Lite-Brite, because we talk about activations. A Lite-Brite, I guess, is not for all age groups, but for our age this is a historical artifact of a life, right?

Kristin: Has it been in any Toy Story movies? Because maybe if they've had a Lite-Brite in Toy Story movies…

Katherine: For those of us that know, we know. And then you're just going to patch some different colors on there, right? To change the experience. And that we can actually do now, extremely optimized and what we call basically in flight. And even though there were bugs in cryptographic code that people use for many years — I'm talking specifically about OpenSSL and Heartbleed, which was a particular attack on encrypted web traffic that was uncovered — the idea is that if things are open, they can be reviewed by many persons. And when things are closed, they can only be reviewed or audited by people either who are paid by the group that has, that owns that software and/or those systems, or by the group itself.

And so when we think of, do we want to certify security — do we want to do that open, closed? And usually the answer from at least the cryptography community has been, we want to try to do that open. Maybe there are some things that are proprietary and closed, but they are not the core algorithms and the core theorems that underpin the security guarantees of cryptography.

Because again, in the nature of science and in the history of science through thousands of years now, we have always made things better and more secure by making them open and then asking people to break them to figure out how they don't work and then continuing again.
