# 三个被表面话题掩盖的系统性真相
## 一、CLARITY 法案的真正杀手，不是加密行业的敌人，而是纽约市长初选
表面上，这是一场"银行 vs 反腐"、"参议员 vs 参议员"的常规立法拉锯。但如果你把节目里 Austin 提到的一个细节放大——"民主党内部的温和派开始害怕远左派掐着他们的脖子，因为纽约那场初选"——你会看到一个反直觉的因果链：**曼达尼在纽约的胜选，正在杀死一部远在华盛顿的加密法案**。
这就是政治学里常被忽视的**"侧翼恐惧传导机制"**：立法者投的不是眼前这张票，而是自己两年后初选时的选民画像。加密行业以为自己在和"反加密派"作战，实际上是被卷入了一场跟自己毫无关系的党内代际战争。
这里有一个和后面 Iran/Ukraine 议题惊人的**跨领域同构**：Yaroslav Trofimov 说"两场战争已经正式合并"。而 CLARITY 法案的困境，是**两场党内战争的合并**——加密监管战 + 民主党路线战。**当独立冲突开始共享同一批人质时，谈判空间就消失了。** 这就是为什么 Poly Market 从 60% 掉到 38%——它不是在给"加密法案

item.title: [Lex Clips] The truth about slavery: It was very profitable in America | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"资产阶级"真相：奴隶制不是在死去，而是在升级

最反直觉的一点藏在那句轻描淡写的话里——1860年，奴隶作为"财产"的估值约 30 亿美元，超过全美所有铁路、所有工业加总（不足 25 亿美元）。这意味着奴隶主不是过时的农业贵族，而是当时美国最大的资产持有阶级，其"资产组合"规模超过整个工业革命在美国的物质结晶。

更惊人的是 Gallagher 顺口提到的一句：奴隶制正在从棉花、稻米、蔗糖的种植农业向工业应用迁移。也就是说，奴隶制不是一台正在报废的旧机器，而是一台正在版本迭代的系统。传统叙事说"奴隶制在经济上注定灭亡，战争多余"——这在数字面前是彻底错误的。它更像今天我们看待石油：明明知道它有问题，但它太赚钱、嵌入太深、正在寻找新的应用场景，所以自我了断的概率接近于零。

跨领域连接：这几乎是一切"路径依赖锁定"的教科书案例——从燃油车产业到社交媒体注意力经济，一个越赚钱的系统越不可能通过内部理性自我终结。道德觉醒从来打不过资产负债表，除非外力介入把资产端强行清零。美国内战本质上是人类史上最大规模的一次强制资产减记——一次 30 亿美元、约合当时 GDP 相当比例的财富被一夜蒸发。

二、"道德距离"的经济学：为什么英国可以体面地废奴

Gallagher 触到了一个几乎所有历史课都跳过的问题：为什么英国 1833 年花钱赎买 80 万奴隶就搞定，美国却要死 75 万人？他给出的答案很朴素——英国被解放的奴隶不住在英国本土。

这一句话打开的洞察远超其字面意义。它揭示了一条跨越两百年的普适规律：道德的成本，与被伤害者的物理距离成反比。

跨领域连接： - 今天我们能心安理得地消费来自遥远工厂的服装和电子产品——因为血汗劳动被"外包"到看不见的地方； - ESG 投资体系热衷于剥离煤矿、烟草，但资本转手就流向新兴市场的同类项目——污染不是消失，是搬家了； - 大型语言模型的数据标注在肯尼亚以每小时 2 美元完成，硅谷才谈得起"AI 伦理"。

南方之所以要用战争抵抗，不是因为他们比北方更邪恶，而是因为他们没有"道德距离"这个奢侈品可以购买。奴隶就住在他们家里、床边、田里。放弃奴隶制不是签一份法案，而是要与曾经的"财产"共享同一片土地和未来——他们真正恐惧的不是经济损失，而是共存。这一点，Gallagher 用一句"a lot of them were afraid of them"轻轻带过，却是整场战争的心理内核。

三、《解放奴隶宣言》的悖论：一份只在"够不着的地方"生效的自由令

最诡异也最少被讨论的历史事实：林肯签署宣言的那一刻，实际上没有解放任何一个人。因为他的宣言只适用于他控制不到的地方——即仍在叛乱中的南方腹地。凡是联邦军已经占领的地区，反而不适用。

这形成了一个近乎卡夫卡式的主权悖论：你能触及的地方你不能解放，你不能触及的地方你才能解放。 自由的边界，就是行军的边界——军队每前进一里，宣言就"追认"一里的自由。

跨领域连接： - 这与现代经济制裁的逻辑同构——制裁令的强度往往与你实际控制力反相关，它是一种"符号性的越界"； - 与国际法的运作类似——它对签约国有效，对真正的作恶者往往无效； - 与代码部署的 feature flag 也奇妙相似——你先声明一个特性存在，等基础设施到位了才真正生效。

Gallagher 提到宣言的语言"平淡得像一张提单（bill of lading）"，这不是林肯没有文采，而是他故意去除道德光环，把它包装成一份纯粹的军事征用文件。因为他清醒地知道：如果这份宣言听起来像道德革命，北方民主党人会立刻撤出战争。他必须让"解放黑人"看起来只是"击垮南方经济"的一个副作用。

这才是真正让人后背发凉的洞察：人类历史上最伟大的解放文件之一，是被刻意去道德化地写出来的——因为在那个时代，没有伪装成军事必要性，就无法通过政治现实这一关。真正推动历史的，往往不是它宣称的理由，而是它藏起来的理由。

📝 转录文本

Setting the Context: Slavery Across Human History

This is perhaps a bit outside the scope of what we'll talk about today, but just to lay out the context on slavery in general in human history, we should say that slavery was ubiquitous. It existed in virtually every major civilization in the history of humans — Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, Rome, China, the Islamic world, Africa, the Americas, North and South America.

The 4% Statistic: Where the Atlantic Slave Trade Actually Went

We should also say something that, as I was looking into this — another big topic — which is the Atlantic slave trade. And it was surprising to me, this stat I wasn't aware of, I would venture to say most Americans probably don't know: that only 4% of African slaves were brought to North America, to the United States. Brazil is the main destination. Brazil, the Caribbean was over 90% — 4.9 million in Brazil, 4 million in the Caribbean. And it was also the last of the states to abolish slave trade.

So, only 4% of the Atlantic slave trade went to the United States. The story of human slavery is one that reaches deep into our history and geographically is much larger than we often study in the context of the United States.

The War as an Accelerator

One thing the war — this Civil War, which I'll just call "the war" for the rest of our discussion — one thing it did was end slavery in 4 years in the United States. Whereas in the absence of that war, it might have gone on for decades. I think the United States would have had the ignominious distinction of being the last place to get rid of slavery. It would have been after Brazil, would have been after Spanish Cuba, because it was thriving in the United States in 1860.

It was making the transition from cash crop agriculture to industrial applications and other applications — growing not just cotton and rice and sugar. There was a time in the literature when people argued that the Civil War was needless because slavery was on its way out. That's absolutely wrong. It was not on its way out. It was thriving. Lincoln said at one point he thought it might have lasted another 50 years, and I don't know how many years it would have lasted, but I think it would have lasted longer than it did in either Cuba or Brazil if the war hadn't taken place.

The Economics: A Flourishing Institution

So, slavery was flourishing in the United States.

Flourishing. From an economics perspective, especially — the wealthiest part. The 1860 census is our friend, and it tells us that the people who controlled the most wealth in the United States were slave holders. And their property in slaves alone — not their other holdings, not their land holdings, just property in slaves — were valued at about $3 billion. The value of all industries, all railroads, all of that put together — fewer than $2.5 billion. So, the people who controlled the most wealth by far were the slave holding class.

So, it was the most valuable industry in the United States, and perhaps it is the reason — again, a bit out of scope, but maybe it helps lay out the land.

Why the US Path Was Different

Let's look at the 19th century. Most slave-owning societies of the era were able to abolish slavery without people dying at the mass scale that we'll discuss:

  • Britain freed 800,000 slaves in 1833 by buying their freedom.
  • Russia freed 23 million serfs in 1861 with a decree — legally.
  • Brazil, which imported more than 10 times as many enslaved Africans as the United States, abolished slavery in 1888 through basic ordinary legislation. No violence.

Why did the US have a Civil War with an estimated 750,000 people dead in order to abolish slavery?

Let's talk just for a second about the 750,000 dead soldiers we're talking about. The number for years was 618,000, and that's been revised lately. I think we're probably certainly more than 700,000 — by far the bloodiest war in our history. As a percentage of the population, off the charts, by far the bloodiest.

I think there's a big difference between Great Britain doing it and the United States doing it: Great Britain did it in play in other places. There weren't millions of enslaved people in Great Britain at the time. For them it might have been a little bit easier to free enslaved people who don't live among you than for the United States. The ante is up for the Confederacy because they enslaved people who lived here, and I think a lot of them were afraid of them and what would happen if they weren't enslaved anymore.

The Shift in War Aims

The war doesn't begin as a war to end slavery. There's a major shift in the war beginning in the summer of 1862, where you add to the war aim. The war aim for the United States initially is to suppress the rebellion, which is what they called this — they didn't call it the Civil War for the most part during the war. It's the "War of the Rebellion." That's the goal initially.

As the war goes on and becomes costlier and more all-encompassing, they decide that they're not going to be able to suppress the rebellion unless they also strike at slavery, because slavery underpins the Confederate war-making capacity. You have enslaved labor that keeps the economy going and allows the Confederacy to mobilize between 85 and 90% of all their white military-age males. It's an astonishing mobilization. It's only possible because enslaved labor keeps the economy going. If you take that enslaved labor away, it deals a significant blow to the Confederate economy — and by extension, to its ability to wage a 19th century war.

The Emancipation Proclamation as Military Strategy

So, the Emancipation Proclamation was in part a military strategy.

Abraham Lincoln based it entirely on his war-making power as commander-in-chief in a time of open rebellion. He's often been criticized for not including the soaring language he was capable of in the Emancipation Proclamation. One historian likened it to a bill of lading — it had all the soaring language of a bill of lading. He did that on purpose.

He did it because he doesn't have the power to strike at slavery in the absence of a war. The president doesn't. And he did it because he knows that he can't win the war with only Republicans in the army. He needs to keep Democrats on board with the war as well. They're not in favor of emancipation. The one way that they might accept it is as a tool to help achieve union. And to do that, we've got to strike at the rebels this way — strike at slavery. That will hurt their war effort, and it will also punish the people who brought on the war.

So, Lincoln hoped that by basing it strictly on his war power, it might be more widely accepted across all parts of the loyal states, and not as controversial as it was. It was still intensely controversial. It alienated many Democrats when he issued it, who said, "You're changing what this war is about. We're willing to shed our blood and maybe risk our lives to restore the union of the founders. I'm not going to risk my life to free a black person." That's a very, very common attitude among Democrats.

What the Proclamation Actually Did

So what did the Emancipation Proclamation actually do? It emphasized the freeing of slaves in the South. It's even more complicated than that.

The only place that Lincoln said he had the power as the war leader to strike at slavery is where the rebels were actually still in rebellion and in control. So, any place where the US Army was in control — any place, he said — that is in essence United States territory. "Now, I can't free them there because I don't have the power. I can only free them where we don't have the power."

So he exempted parts of states and areas in the South that it didn't apply to as of the moment he signed it. Going forward, any place that the United States Army went — where it hadn't been on January 1st, 1863 — the Emancipation Proclamation applied, and enslaved people would be freed by it. Literally at the time he signed it, he didn't free anybody, because he's only saying: "I can free them where we're not in control. We have to be in control for this to have effect, for this to have power."

The Army as the Boundary of Freedom

So, in part, this is why the army was the boundary at which the freeing was happening. It's absolutely the boundary.

And Congress had already passed what was called the Second Confiscation Act. It passed this in July of 1862, that announced that all enslaved people belonging to rebels were free. It didn't apply to people who could prove they were unionists living in the South, and all states. Lincoln didn't make that distinction in the Emancipation Proclamation. His proclamation is broader than the Second Confiscation Act was.

item.title: [Zhang Xiaojun Podcast] You Kaichao: vLLM, Open-Source Infra, Model Co-Design & Journey from Community to Startup
item.dc:creator: Zhang Xiaojun Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的发现：开源社区的"贵族性"，恰恰源于博士训练制度的中段真空

大多数人以为开源项目靠"热情"和"社区精神"驱动，但游凯超讲的一个细节暴露了一个更冷峻的结构性真相：博士第一年要做新东西不能维护老项目，博士末期忙着找工作不能维护老项目，只有"博士中后段、已经发过论文、暂无毕业压力"的极窄窗口——这才是开源项目最优质的劳动力池。

换句话说，vLLM 的诞生并非"社区的胜利"，而是Berkeley 精心校准的博士生命周期与一个新兴技术窗口的时间套利。David Patterson 那句"实验室生命周期就是五年（一届博士）"点破了本质：伯克利的 AMPLab → RISELab → SkyLab 每五年一换、每一届都能诞生一个 Spark 或 Ray 或 vLLM——这不是巧合，这是用博士的青春折旧曲线做产业级的开源投资。

有意思的是：这个模式在中国基本无法复制。中国的博士培养、毕业压力、就业焦虑分布都不同，"中段真空"根本不存在。所以中国的开源不是没有热情，是没有那个可以合法"耍废两年做世界级基础设施"的制度性缝隙。

二、跨领域连接：Token 不是电力，而是"带指纹的电"——这是能源史上从未有过的商品形态

游凯超反复用"发电—用电"类比推理系统。但他自己在访谈末段撕开了这个类比：电压可以在插座端统一转换成 220V，token 却带着模型指纹，无法在出口标准化。

这是一个惊人的观察。你可以把它翻译到别的行业： - 原油可以炼成汽油再卖给任何车——中间层能标准化； - 电力可以变压变频再进入任何家电——出口能标准化； - Token 是历史上第一种"从生产到消费全链路都保留生产者指纹的商品"——它更像是"艺术品级别的能源"，或者说更像中世纪的手抄本：每一份都因抄写者而异，没有印刷术的标准化。

这带来一个更深的推论：AI 推理系统的商业形态，本质上更接近"电网调度 + 老字号餐厅前厅"的混合体，而不是云计算的一般化。这也解释了为什么 vLLM 一定要支持 200+ 模型——因为每一种模型就是一种"方言电"，你必须懂它的电压、频率、脉冲形状才能让它上网。这个世界不是趋向统一，而是趋向"标准化的多样性管理"。

三、被忽略的隐藏真相：Deepseek 的 Infra 优势不来自 AI，而来自"量化基金对纳秒的病态执念"

游凯超那句"Deepseek 的深厚 infra 底子可能来自他们做量化交易时对性能的极致压榨"值得单独放大。

主流叙事把 Deepseek 的成功归因于开源精神、聪明的算法学生、MoE 创新。但真正的技术跨领域连接是：高频量化交易的"纳秒工程"文化，在被移植到 LLM 训练时，制造了一个其他 AI 公司无法复制的护城河。

量化交易在过去二十年被逼着做的事： - 从上到下控制整个栈（自建集群、自研网络协议、自研 FPGA/ASIC） - 对每一微秒延迟做经济价值折算 - 系统工程师和策略研究员坐在一张桌子上（算法学生懂 infra 的文化根源）

这三件事是硅谷 AI 大厂做不到的——因为大厂的 infra 团队和算法团队隔着六层组织墙。这也解释了游凯超那句更微妙的话："其他大厂能给他 20M/年 offer，也做不出 Deepseek 的东西"——这不是钱的问题，是组织基因的问题。

一个大胆预测：未来五年，真正做出下一代 LLM Infra 突破的团队，可能不是纯 AI 公司，而是具有"每毫秒有经济含义"训练背景的领域迁移者——除了量化基金，也许还包括：卫星实时信号处理团队、超算气象模拟团队、甚至游戏引擎团队。这些人天生就理解"performance is a first-class product feature"，这是 web/mobile 时代长大的工程师体会不到的世界观。

再进一步：游凯超说"算法应该主动靠近 infra"——但这句话的隐含前提是硬件已经被浇筑。而当 Deepseek 那种"从芯片到策略全栈控制"的团队多起来，可能会出现相反的钟摆：算法团队反向定义下一代硬件。这也是为什么 Deepseek 招 Agent 框架人不奇怪——他们要把整条链路（硬件 → 模型 → Harness → Agent）全部纳入 co-design，做一个真正的"垂直集成的 AI 拟态生物"。而 vLLM 选择做"通用发电—并网系统"，正好卡在互补生态位。这两条路线不会互相消灭，而会像 iOS vs Android、Linux vs Windows 那样长期共存。

Test time scaling has always existed. It only appears in different forms. In the early machine learning system, we have an integrated learning method called ensemble. You can ask different models to answer the same question, or you can ask the same model to answer multiple times, and then integrate the results. Usually, you can see a better improvement. In this test time scaling, the scale is the number of attempts.

And then, the test time scaling in the big model era, more generally refers to the open eye, the O1, the problem of difficulty. We can improve the success rate by allowing the model to think for a longer time. What we scale in here is the token output of the model. So last year, we often saw models thinking for a long time, and then outputting tens of thousands of tokens to solve some high-difficulty problems. For example, international math competitions.

Of course, these are all very effective methods. But since this year, our test time scaling has been more in the context of coding agents, allowing agents to continue to interact with the environment. At this time, what we scale is the number of models interacting with the environment, or the time it takes for the model to complete a task, In this process, the model's thinking is relatively short every time it is delivered. It may only have a few hundred tokens, but it can continuously understand the environment in which the current task is located, and adapt some of the characteristics of this environment to make it more efficient in completing the task.

Let's not talk about the advanced learning. This is a very early machine learning method. It doesn't match the current model. So why did I say before that I deleted Beam Search?

Then, later, it was a big explosion this year. Through the exploration of the environment, Coding Agent can adapt to various environments. So it can enter people's daily lives. For example, the hot trend of crayfish in the beginning of the year.

Under this multi-person exchange, pre-precision caching is also called pre-precision caching. It is very important. We must try to ensure that the historical status can be preserved. So that the next request can be made quickly. So the test and scaling stages have different requirements for the push engine.

This way, the push engine can use the previous calculations. Of course, there are some models that are not completely adhering to the premise stability at the beginning of the design. For example, some models will delete the previous thinking process when thinking about the next round. At this point, we need to do some joint optimization with the push engine.

Different harness frames will have different load characteristics. And different model structures will have different need for rationalization. So it's hard to unify. This is similar to the problem of infra code design. What we need now is a harness and infra code design.

In this regard, last year, Manas' Geek, Peak, also wrote a blog about how to design an infra-friendly harness frame. The most important part is to fully utilize the preload storage. Some of the Harness framework designers may be more smart than others, and think that every time they refine the tool range, they can improve the model efficiency. But in fact, because the tool is always on the front end of the model request, this operation will lead to the result that every request will not be able to reuse the previous calculation. So this brings a huge burden to the reasoning system.

Then there are some ancient traditions, such as chat GPT. It will add the current date in the system prompt before. So the pre-due memory will fail when the date is changed. This is also a very bad behavior. The more elegant way is to use the date as a tool for the model. If the model thinks it needs the date, it can check the date. So, don't put a frequently changed thing in the front of the request.

The most extreme example is the harness frame. It puts the current time into the request, and it's accurate to the second. And its time task is always set to the whole point. This will lead to a huge flow of the system receiving a huge amount of the pressure. This will also cause a huge amount of pressure on the system. A very well-known saying by Munchard is that a group of crayfish will attack the moon together.

Deepseq has recently completed a large round of financing and is also expanding its business. You can see that the first position it has been hired for is the position related to the framework design of Agents. So I'm looking forward to seeing what kind of framework Deepseq can put forward. They are on the same page in terms of model and infra code design. I also believe that their framework, the harness framework, can reach the same level as the infra code design. And then give the community a chance to say, "This is a good framework for agents."

模型与芯片的深度协同

You mentioned the agent framework, HANIS, and infra, and their co-design. Some people say that in the future AI systems, the model and chip architecture will be more and more harmonious. Just like Apple's M chip and iOS, do you agree? What does this mean to you in terms of the general framework?

The trend is that the structure of the model and the chip structure are getting more and more in harmony. And the model is leaning towards the chip because the chip is designed that way. If you don't lean towards the chip, your efficiency will be greatly reduced.

I'll mention David Patterson again. He gave a speech when he won the Turing Prize. He talked about his views on the structure of the computer. There are two main points in this.

The first is that the Moe law cannot be continued. The general computing power cannot continue to rise. So, if you want to achieve higher performance, the only way out is to design specific chip structures in the field. That is, provide special chips for specific load. On the other hand, this further restricts the chip design. It is designed for this load. If your model is not designed like this, you will not be able to enjoy the popularity of the chip.

Second, the proof-of-conceal is simple but effective. When the chip structure is optimized for a specific load, we naturally ask whether the specific load is so important and worth optimizing. The development history of Invida and the exploration experience of the industrial world over the past 20 years show that the special load of the array of proofs is so effective. As long as you can calculate the array of proofs quickly, many problems can be solved. So these two points may be complementary, which leads to the high-performance computing chips now basically becoming the calculation unit of the array of proofs. So the design of the model structure must also be as close as possible to the array of proofs.

FP8 量化案例

I can give you a specific example. For example, the design of the F18's quantified format. In the years of 1924 and 1925, the Inuita's flagship chip was converted from A100 to H100, and then upgraded from the Amper architecture to the Hopper architecture. One of the major selling points of the Hopper architecture is the computing power of the F18, which is 8 bits of floating point computing. It can be twice as fast as 16 bits of floating point computing.

DeepSeq should be the first large-scale FP8 training team. Their core is block quantization. For the whole, it's block quantization. For activation, it's true channel quantization. This design also fits the next generation of chips, the MX quantization format.

Of course, pure block quantization cannot solve this problem. Some of the teams have explored this before. They found that this method actually has a precision problem in the calculation of the argument. So it became the second step in their path. But after DeepSeq explored the method of collection, they used a large number of units to build a cluster. They used the features of two parts of the chip to perform at the same time, and achieved the advantage of the performance of the computing efficiency without loss. So they took the lead over other competitors. These stories can be publicly investigated. They are all written in the DBG's technical report. It's just how many people read it. Different people will draw different points.

给 Infra 团队的建议

If you want to give some suggestions to the team that wants to do well in infra, what might be the secret sauce? Are there any ways or methodological levels?

I think the core of this is to think from the perspective of the principle of the first. That is, our so-called first principle. Because the AI industry is very hot, and there are many entrepreneurs in the industry, every topic, every month, may have ten new technologies that have been created. These need a technical team to think from the perspective of the principle of the first. Which technologies are useful? Which technologies are just a waste of time?

Let's not forget about the heat dissipation, power consumption, hardware frequency, and the impact on performance. If you do performance optimization, you may get lucky. If you improve performance, you will get lucky. For example, when it comes to model structure design, some students don't even know the calculation process under various batching conditions. They only know the formula in the textbooks, and don't know how to write Flash Attention.

So, I think one of the most important conditions for a team is to have enough people in the team to think from the perspective of the first-person perspective, what kind of problem they need to solve. And then under this premise, different teams may have different hardware environments or different resource limitations, and made all kinds of choices. That's reasonable. But I think as long as they think from the perspective of the first-person principle to solve the problem, their results will not be bad.

And then I'll give you another example. I transferred from algorithmic research to machine learning system research. So I'm sure I'm not as good as students who have been in the industry for many years. But when I was learning about GPU kernel programming, the first thing I looked at was the GPU's programming model. What design spaces did it provide me with?

After understanding these first-person principles, I soon found a very painful problem, which is an illegal memory access on the GPU. This is a very difficult problem to solve in the GPU kernel. But when I understood the GPU kernel from the principle of the first nature, I soon found a technology called CUDA Core Dump. This technology has existed for a long time, but very few people in the AI infra circle know about it. After I learned about the GPU's programming structure, I realized that there should be a tool for programming. The GPU drive should be able to support such tasks. So I continued to ask the team at Invitada about the solution. They finally found it. The solution already existed, but no one knew about it. After I promoted the solution in the community, it solved a lot of difficulties.

So, in a fast-growing stage, we need to use the principle of the first nature to see the main line of the development of this era, and then to block the noise and continue to invest in a useful direction. I think this is the most important.

未来趋势预测

Based on the model structure and the infra code design concept, What is the eye direction of the two lines of the infra and the model structure? Can you make some technical predictions?

This is difficult to predict because the development of the model structure is not a linear forward. It is more likely to be a spiral-like rise. And sometimes it may also go to some curves. And the model structure and infra are not all, right? Sometimes it is served to the corresponding needs.

In individual fields, such as biological chemistry, they deal with some special data. In natural sciences, they may need thousands of upper and lower layers, even one-level upper and lower layers. But dealing with this model, I think its upper and lower layers should no longer need to be greatly increased. In the process of performing long-term tasks, or some needs for lifelong learning, I think they can be realized through external tools, such as memory modules, some skill modules, or through some sub-agent modules.

I think they should be fine. For example, it's summer now, and we're in the peak of power consumption. We can't say that the power generation will be ruined. The power generation will have to work harder to generate more electricity. So the growth of the explosive-type tokens that are needed for the push is more urgent for the demand for the efficiency of the push.

Because the resources on Earth are limited, so is the overall computing power. The power supply is also limited. So when we encounter difficulties, we need to think of a way. For example, the harness framework we mentioned earlier can do some co-design with the push engine. The same task and reasonable harness design can allow the push engine to generate more tokens.

People will be flexible and change their way of thinking. If there are not enough tokens, people will start to study how to save tokens. When there is not enough money, people will study how to use some cheaper models to do the same thing. So I think overall, this is a very exciting era. So many smart minds are pushing for the development of AI. So I believe we will definitely achieve a token balance.

Of course, we need to work together on both sides. On the supply side, we need to optimize and increase the efficiency of production. On the demand side, we need to plan more to increase the efficiency of the token.

So efficiency and effect don't conflict.

Yes, they must make a common progress.

中美开源格局

Are they faster overseas and faster in efficiency? Yes, that's my feeling.

China's opening culture is now in place. Do you think China's opening ecosystem has had a profound impact on the global model?

I think China's opening has had a profound impact on the world. Basically, after the US went to the edge, it took on the opening momentum. So it's very important and it's done very well.

Are there many open source communities in the US?

The US is mainly a technical community for open source reasoning. The model is not open source. Some companies are also open source, like Mistra. And then there are other ones like Poseidon. There are not many that we know of, but there are some companies that are opening up. But there are no top-level ones at the moment.

Will this lead your business center to move to China?

We are mainly doing business in North America. Because the model is opening up in China, but it can be used in North America.

What do you think the competition between China and the US in AI infrastructure will be like? Can you make some predictions?

I don't think they are competing. They are all at different heights and different places. For example, China is clearly lacking in high-end computing power. So it needs to find ways to use all kinds of capable computing power. So it will focus more on the adaptation of domestic cards. Its advantage is that the supply of land and computing power The supply of land and electricity is more than enough. So there's no problem with establishing a data center. The U.S. has more advanced computing power. It doesn't have the same kind of chip. But there's a problem with land and electricity supply. So they're now bringing in electricity supply.

模型能力的护城河

What do you think the direction of the model of China-US relations will be?

I think we should use electricity as an example. Token and electricity have similarities and differences. For example, when it comes to power generation, if you have a nuclear power plant, you can supply electricity to a city with the power that the nuclear power plant produces. If the city uses this electricity for a lifetime, it won't be able to research nuclear power. It's just electricity. It won't touch the technology.

But the big model is different. The big model is all about the model. The model needs to be used. Once you've used it for a long time, the user can train the model. So a model is not something that can be hidden from users for a long time. So for a long time, the cost of training a model will definitely drop. Because everyone can collect their own data. Especially after the coding agent came, right?

Yes, especially the coding agent data. You can collect it quickly. I think usually in a month or so, a company-level institution can collect enough training data. So at this time, its internal wheels can turn and it can train its own model.

Which companies are already starting to make their own fairies? Like G.O.M. 5.2, they are doing very well.

This has something to do with the data they collect?

I'm not sure how they do it specifically, but I think they must have some advantages in data collection.

So this will bring the advantage of the leading party, right? Yes, this will bring the advantage of the leader. But I think this advantage is certainly not long-term. Like I said, I think the advantage of model capability is that it can't be held for long.

What is the last barrier?

I think in the current scenario, the barrier comes more from whether you can quickly fall. So there is nothing you can hold for a year. You must be able to constantly push forward. The last model will be a I think it will win in the end. Because I think the open-source model will win in the end. So when the model is open, everyone can use it.

So you bet on China?

I bet on the open-source model. If the Chinese model opens, I support the Chinese model. If the other countries' models open, I support them too.

When did this idea come about?

I think this is based on the understanding of AI. From the perspective of the first principle, a model is not something that can be hidden for a long time. It's not like a nuclear weapon. Once you've studied it, you only need to explode it once to show it to others. Then you can hide it and use it to intimidate others. A model is a civilized technology. It must be used on a large scale. So from the perspective of the first principle of AI, you can give everyone a large-scale use, and everyone can collect data on a large scale. Then this model will inevitably be copied.

开源模型对 vLLM 的意义

If the open-air model wins, will it have an impact on your company? Will it have an impact on VLM?

That's a good thing for us. So our company is focusing on reasoning. We think that someone will help us solve the model problem.

Will the model companies do their own reasoning?

Yes, they will do their own reasoning.

Then why do they need VLM?

This is because their internal push engine is often difficult to deploy externally. So, for example, Deepseq's infrastructure is very strong. But this is based on their complete ability to control their own conditions from the group to the upper layer of software. So they can't do rapid expansion. For example, if you give them a 10x machine, can they immediately generate a 10x token? This is not possible.

And then the open source reasoning we do is more of a more functional reasoning. For example, I can rent some machines on the cloud. Maybe this machine has all kinds of restrictions. Maybe we can't control it that well. But we can also make a reasonable reasoning engine.

Do you think you will be the next Linux?

We are considering this. Or we are indeed developing this. And I think its influence We can already say that it is Linux in the AI reasoning field. For example, you see that one of the important maintenance companies in Linux is Red Hat. It has promoted Linux. Red Hat is also investing in VLM. Why is it investing in VLM? It thinks that VLM is the next Linux. It has already packed VLM into many of their Linux enterprise distribution boards. So when they deploy in the future, it will no longer be a cold operating system, but an AI operating system that can operate AI.

Do you have any financing plans in the future?

Yes, our company will definitely continue to finance. But I think, as I said before, we are not financing for financing. We mostly hope to have some results that we think are worth financing. So we are working on a number of projects.

Where is the next milestone?

The next milestone is more internal. We hope to open up some business models and create some business models that can be expanded. I think that's when we will be investing again.

个人特质与写作

I think you have more passion than I thought, especially for your open community. I feel that you also like to do the same things, solve common problems, and make a transparent system. How do you think your character is formed?

嗯。This is also a trend that has only been around for the past decade or so. I grew up in such an environment, so I naturally think that technology is a natural thing.

In your experience in the US, do Chinese people or teams have more enthusiasm for opening up compared to other countries and regions? I don't know if I'm asking the right question.

I think this may not have much to do with the country. This is an open source movement in the global scope. It started to open up from decades ago, and has evolved into the state it is today. It started to open up from 2016.

Why do you like writing? What do you think writing and writing and interaction with the world bring to you?

I have a lot of technical creation. My writing is also technical creation. So I think I can integrate it into the field of open source. Open source is not necessarily a algorithm. It also includes some technical knowledge sharing. It's a process of communicating freely with the community.

Are you someone who thinks through writing?

But some people think through writing, some people think through words. Sometimes, people who write don't have such strong ability to express themselves. I don't think you have this problem.

I think writing and speaking are similar. I want to express my thoughts clearly. Of course, I also like math and physics, so I like to form it. You can only verify things if you write them down. You need to guess boldly, but be careful to correct. So you have to put your language into words and then polish it.

Do you manage your team through a lot of text?

We have a lot of text because we have two bases in Singapore and the US. So we can't be together for a long time. So we communicate through text or online meetings.

Do you write a long text together?

长文档的方式比较少,更多就是直接比如说在 Slack 里面聊天吧。

给年轻研究者的建议

对于现在想要入行的年轻的 AI Researcher 你会有些什么样的建议吗?

It's not a good time to enter the industry. The competition is getting heated up and people are feeling down. It's hard to accumulate something stable for a long time. So I can only say that I personally agree that doing things from the perspective of the principle of the first nature. It's the same as being a person, right? Just figure out what you want and then work hard. And then I think that generally from this perspective, the end result will not be too bad.

系统的重要性再确认

I've seen you say that in the era of the Homo Erdogan, the upper limit of AI depends on the system, not the algorithm. Do you still agree with this concept today?

  • Attention is all you need.
  • decoding.

So when it was first proposed, everyone said it was very slow because you can only calculate tokens one by one. The efficiency is very low, so it must be useless. But after these years of development, After seeing the auto-regressive decoding, we have made a lot of improvements on it. For example, one of the important improvements is the continuous batching technology combined with the Pager Attention technology. This reduces the cost of auto-regressive decoding. There is also another very important technology, which is spec decoding. We can turn each token's decoding into a small token verification. This is also a system for the change in the algorithm.

In the previous blog, we also mentioned linear attention. So, there are many people who are studying what kind of linear tension is good and suitable. The key is what Manbato and Songlin have proposed. It should be the Trunk-Peril algorithm that Songlin proposed. It's how you can calculate in segments and then you can have some efficient computing methods in the process of segmentation.

So, this series is actually about how to support algorithms better at the system level. It also means that there is a system lottery problem. Can your algorithm be achieved by the system? Only the algorithm that is achieved by the system can stay. So the system is very important.

It's also a lottery. Yes, because this is a very special era. Everyone needs code design because the general progress is gone. So you need to code design with hardware, you need to code design with systems, and you need to code design with harness. So overall, this is a very fast-changing era. And your code design can also bring more space to your development.

So the code design can only solve a problem for a period of time, it can't solve a longer problem.

历史与人类文明

From the history of human beings, what do you think is the current state of affairs?

It is indeed at a technical point. Since the revival of civilization, human history has been Technology is constantly accumulating. This is a terrible thing. It's a curve of growth in numbers. Each generation is exploring further based on the previous generation's technology. Each generation has improved the previous generation's technology.

Now, with the advent of computer technology, We can not only accumulate on the past's technology, but we can even take the past's thoughts, words, and life and then we can add them to the history of all people and then we can make a digital-level growth. This is the emergence of AI. We have a lot of Internet language. We can basically use the entire human history to train. So that's where AI was born. So it's really about the development of indexes.

Many people are discussing how to coexist carbon and carbon-based machines. What do you think your life will be like?

This is hard to imagine. But I personally feel that... ...the Tanki and the Gui are both good at their own thing. Especially when I was working on the system, I found that... ...the Gui's intelligence is more of a summary. It's what he learned from the language he learned. and then humans can still provide some insight. Or we can have more context, and we can provide more useful suggestions. In ideal circumstances, of course, humans can cultivate this collective intelligence to make the world a better place.

I think this is an unimaginable problem. You have to observe fate first, then you believe it. I don't see any means of observing fate. Maybe when you were dreaming, you had your own fate. I haven't had such a flash in the pan yet.

快问快答

Let's have some quick questions.

全球范围内最喜欢的美食？

I don't really like food. I'm not very interested in food.

全球范围内喜欢的地方？

I'm impressed by Berkeley. I've been there for two important changes in my life. I've been there for my bachelor's and my master's.

需要知道的知识？

I'll talk about the knowledge of the push engine. There are many big models. I'm not saying it's absolute. But if you input 1000感叹号 to a big model, it will output many感叹号. Sometimes you can use this to detect the push engine behind it. It has a few steps of speculation. So you can use the token to reverse the push engine's technology.

喜欢的音乐？

I think that in today's context, I'll just say a few words about Li Zongsheng. There's a phrase in there that says, "I want to say it, but I haven't said it yet." So we can talk about it later if we have time.

影响 AI 的重要论文？

I think we've talked about a lot of these. For example, the Transformers and the GBG3 papers. I might start with the technical part. From a system engineering perspective, I would add that the Flash Attention, the VLM, and the Flash Linear Attention that I mentioned earlier, they all greatly affected the progress of these technologies.

关键的 BAT？

Based on your current understanding of a key BAT, what is it?

I think the key BAT I mentioned earlier is the open source model.

关于节目名字的联想

Our studio is called the Language and World Studio. When you first heard the name, what were you thinking?

"The world of languages" is what Wittgenstein said. "The limit of my language is the limit of my world." The first thing that came to my mind when I heard this was that the formula of five-levels can't be expressed in a limited number of four-fold operations and open-source code. The world of languages may just mean that we are a low-level creature, and that there are higher-level creatures outside of us.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的发现：开源社区的"贵族性"，恰恰源于博士训练制度的中段真空
大多数人以为开源项目靠"热情"和"社区精神"驱动，但游凯超讲的一个细节暴露了一个更冷峻的结构性真相：**博士第一年要做新东西不能维护老项目，博士末期忙着找工作不能维护老项目，只有"博士中后段、已经发过论文、暂无毕业压力"的极窄窗口——这才是开源项目最优质的劳动力池**。
换句话说，vLLM 的诞生并非"社区的胜利"，而是**Berkeley 精心校准的博士生命周期与一个新兴技术窗口的时间套利**。David Patterson 那句"实验室生命周期就是五年（一届博士）"点破了本质：伯克利的 AMPLab → RISELab → SkyLab 每五年一换、每一届都能诞生一个 Spark 或 Ray 或 vLLM——这不是巧合，这是**用博士的青春折旧曲线做产业级的开源投资**。
有意思的是：这个模式在中国基本无法复制。中国的博士培养、毕业压力、就业焦虑分布都不同，"中段真空"根本不存在。所以中国的开源不是没有热情，是**没有那个可以合法"耍废两年做世界级基础设施"的制度性缝隙**。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"储备耗尽悖论"：为什么"没崩溃"本身才是崩溃前奏

大多数观察者把"油价没暴涨、供应链没断裂"当作 Rickards 预测失灵的证据。但这里藏着一个反直觉的系统性真相：正是"表面平稳"消耗了系统最后的缓冲。战略石油储备、化肥储备、氦气储备——这些都是"看不见的减震器"。当所有玩家（中国烧更多煤、美国增出口、俄罗斯补缺口、各国动储备）齐心协力"维持假象"时，他们并没有解决问题，而是把弹簧压到了极限。

这让我想起 2008 年金融危机前的"大缓和"（Great Moderation）——恰恰是"稳定"本身孕育了脆弱性。Minsky 的金融不稳定假说在地缘政治层面复演了：稳定期越长，参与者越倾向于消耗冗余，直到系统失去自我修复能力。当下我们看到的"没什么大事发生"，本质上是一场沉默的库存清算。

二、跨领域连接：AI 的"泥浆污染"与生态学中的"自身中毒效应"

Rickards 提到 AI 模型训练互联网数据、然后自己的产出又污染互联网、再被下一代模型吸入——这个"slop 循环"其实是生态学中"自身毒素累积"（autotoxicity）现象的信息论翻版。在森林生态系统里，某些树种会分泌抑制自身幼苗生长的化学物质，导致连作衰退。在土壤微生物学里叫"再植障碍"。

令人意外的观察：AI 泡沫的破裂机制可能不是经济学的（估值过高、债务违约），而是热力学的——一个开放系统若持续向自身反馈熵，最终会因信息质量降解而失去输出价值。这意味着 Rickards 说的"3600 亿美元 AI 债务"背后真正的定时炸弹，不是利率、不是收入，而是训练语料的"信息熵中毒速率"。这是一个可测量但几乎无人在跟踪的指标。

三、金价的"分形回撤"与你系统里更深的一层规律

Rickards 引用 Mandelbrot 的尺度不变性（scale invariance）——10 年图和 1 周图长得一样——来解释 25% 回撤是正常的。但这里有个他没点破的更深层次含义：如果价格波动是分形的，那么"信念的回撤"也是分形的。

散户看到跌 25% 就恐慌，机构看到跌 25% 是加仓机会，央行看到跌 25% 是战略窗口——同样的波动，在不同"时间尺度的持有者"眼中意义完全相反。这就是为什么"金价的散户恐慌"和"央行净买入"能同时存在。

跨领域连接：这与神经科学里的"多时间尺度处理"（multi-timescale processing）惊人相似——大脑不同区域处理毫秒、秒、分钟、小时级信息，同一事件在不同脑区被赋予不同意义。市场是一个"多时间尺度记忆系统"。判断你自己在哪个时间尺度上思考，比预测价格更重要。

四、被隐藏的元洞见：Rickards 整个访谈的"沙漏结构"

回头看整场对话——从霍尔木兹海峡到黄金到 AI 到白银到中国——所有话题在结构上都是同一个形状：一个储备/缓冲被慢慢消耗的沙漏。石油储备在耗尽、美元流动性在耗尽、AI 的"注意力资本"在耗尽、央行黄金库存的透明度在耗尽、Fed 前瞻指引的可信度在耗尽。

真正的洞察不是任何一个预测，而是这个共同结构：我们正处于一个多系统的同步储备耗尽期（synchronized reserve depletion）。当多个独立系统的缓冲同时接近零，它们之间原本微弱的耦合会突然变强——这是复杂系统中"关联性风暴"的经典前兆（correlation storms，2008 年"一切资产同时下跌"就是这个）。

这暗示了一个操作性判断：未来最赚钱的不是猜哪个系统先崩，而是识别系统之间从"独立"变成"耦合"的那个瞬间。

衰退 vs. 萧条：一个被忽视的区别

People focus very much on the word "recession". At least in the US, the rule of thumb is two consecutive quarters of declining GDP. That's a recession. Some are longer than others, some are shallow, some are deep, but that's the basic rule.

We have not had two consecutive quarters of declining GDP. It goes up and down. It's not particularly high at the moment. And so people go, "Well, there's no recession. What are you talking about?"

I would say two things. Number one, where if there's a recession — and I expect there will be — it will be a technical recession within a depression. And a depression is a different thing.

The definition of a depression is growth below trend or below potential, with neither a tendency to collapse nor to return to potential. In other words, if your potential growth is say 3.5% — and I think that is reasonable for a developed economy like the US, and for that matter developed economies in Europe — so if your potential's 3.5% and you're growing between 2 and 2.5%, which we have been on average since 2007, you're in a depression.

You don't have negative growth. Your GDP is not going down, but you're nowhere near your potential, and that gap between the potential growth and the actual growth is lost wealth.

So I would say the US has been in a long depression since 2007. Japan has been in a long depression since 1990. We've seen these kinds of 20-, 30-year depressions — in Japan's case maybe 40 years. They've happened before, in the late 19th century for example.

From 2009 to 2019, for example — from the end of the great global financial crisis to the beginning of the COVID pandemic, a 10-year period — average annual GDP growth in the United States was 2.2%. Well, that kind of proves my point. If your potential is 3.5 and you're growing at 2.2, that's a depression. That's trillions of dollars of lost wealth. We're still in that mode. So that hasn't changed.

Jim Rogers 与 Mandelbrot：波动的两种语言

I talked to Jim Rogers about this years ago — probably the greatest commodities trader of all time. And he said to me — this was when gold had peaked, the earlier peak was about $1,900 an ounce in August 2011, we were talking around 2013, gold had come down a lot — Jim said to me:

"Nothing goes to the moon without a 50% drawdown along the way. That's just how commodities trade. And if you don't know that or you're not prepared for that, you should not be in that commodity."

Then we can take a look at fractal mathematics — basically Mandelbrot — and he introduced a concept called scale invariance. What it says: in volatile systems, if I gave you a one-week chart and I gave you a 10-year chart, and I just took out the timeline so you're looking at two charts with whatever scale, whatever timeline, but you don't know which is which — the charts are the same.

In other words, the volatility you see in a 10-year chart repeats on a daily basis. That's what we mean by scale invariance.

So taking Jim Rogers's point, which I think is exactly right, and applying it to the current context on a smaller scale — because we're starting not from $250 an ounce, but $1,800 an ounce — that's what we're seeing. We're seeing one of those drawdowns.

Now based on that, how low could it go? My estimate — I'm not, this is not a forecast — but it wouldn't surprise me to see gold go to $3,600 an ounce. That would be a full 50% drop from the prior base of $1,800 as I described. That's what the math would say. That's what history would say. Won't necessarily get there, but that's a pretty hard floor. 供给侧通胀 vs. 需求拉动通胀：临界点将至

通胀的三大成因

Inflation has really three main causes:

  1. Supply-side breakdown. Supply chains break down, you have scarcity of goods, the shelves are empty. That by itself is enough to bid up the price.

  2. Higher energy prices flowing through everything. It's not just gas at the pump. Everything moves by fuel — if not gasoline, diesel. Everything you see in the store, everything that gets delivered to your house got there by a truck, and trucks run on diesel. And diesel prices are going up faster than the gasoline prices. But it's not just the shipper has to pay more; they raise the price of everything being transported to make up for the fact that diesel prices are higher. So that feeds inflation through basically all goods and services.

    But at that point, that tends to be self-correcting. Prices get high — people pay more for gas at the pump, so you cut back somewhere else. You don't go out to dinner. You don't take a vacation. You don't buy new clothes. It's inelastic demand. Because of that, you tend to get layoffs, higher unemployment, and recession.

  3. Demand-pull inflation (the tipping point). People's expectations go up: "Hey, this inflation isn't going away, it's getting worse, and I was thinking of buying a refrigerator, I was thinking of buying some new furniture — I better do it now before the price goes up." So you're pulling demand forward, and that kind of psychological, behavioral process drives prices.

Shutting down inflation coming from the supply side is relatively easy — it tends to shut itself down. But shutting down inflation from the demand side is much more difficult because it's behavioral and psychological. It's not like a knob on monetary policy that you can just fix. From that you'll get much higher interest rates, and that will drive the price of gold a lot higher.

70 年代的历史回音

So gold has been going up on some fundamental vectors we described. It hasn't yet hitched onto the inflation bandwagon because that tipping point over to changed expectations has not happened yet. But we're right on the edge. It's very close to happening.

I lived through that in the 70s. I saw it firsthand. The 70s were the same thing: - 1973: inflation was a supply-side shock. - 1974: a really bad recession, stock market crash. - 1976, 1977, 1978: that was all demand-driven. - 1980–1981: inflation in the US got to 15%, and that was when Volcker took interest rates to 20%.

We'll see how it plays out, but that's a driver of higher gold prices. It hasn't really kicked in yet, and I expect it will.

Alex: How do you expect Kevin Warsh from now onwards to be able to change monetary guidance in terms of forward guidance, and the impact it will have on the US economy?

FOMC 的结构

The Fed — technically the Federal Open Market Committee — sets interest rates or interest rate targets. That's the seven members of the Board of Governors and five regional Reserve Bank presidents, including the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, in rotation, except New York always has a seat. So it's a 12-person FOMC that sets rates.

They come out with a statement when they have these meetings every six or seven weeks. Warsh has already shortened the statement. These things used to be like a thousand words. Now they're like 300 words. You might get it down to like a couple sentences.

消灭"点阵图"

They're going to get rid of the dots.

The dots are — there are 12 members of the FOMC, but there are 19 people in the room: 12 regional Reserve Bank presidents and 7 members of the Board of Governors. And they all give these forecasts — unemployment, inflation, interest rates, GDP growth, etc. They put them on a dot chart and combine them. They don't tell you who's who, although you can guess. They're always wrong. I told my readers, "You know, they're there, you can look at them, they'll talk about them on CNBC, but don't use them as a forecast because they're always wrong."

Again, Warsh understands that. He's going to get rid of the dots.

一段个人的 Fed 记忆

I used to talk to the Fed every day. In the late 80s and early 90s, I was on the executive committee of one of the largest primary dealers. The primary dealers — it's a group of about 20 banks that trade with the Fed. I should put it differently: the Fed trades with them. You're on the approved list. So when the Open Market Operations desk at the Federal Reserve Bank in New York wants to pick up the phone, buy and sell securities with banks, they only trade with certain banks. You have to be on that list, and my firm was one of them.

We talked to the Fed all the time. I used to go down there — New York and Washington, but primarily New York — and meet with their officials. In those days, they didn't tell you anything. There was no press conference. There was no statement. The minutes were released years after the fact.

The only way you knew what the Fed was doing was if you traded with them. The traders could look at the bids and offers and say, "Okay, it looks like they're tightening interest rates," and then eventually it would leak out. But for 3 or 4 days, you had this enormous trading advantage because if you were trading with the Fed, you knew what the Fed was doing. But that was the only way you knew.

The other way was — there's a place called Harry's of Hanover Square. It's a bar very close to the Fed headquarters. You could go down there, have a few drinks, and pick up information. That's how you learned about Fed policy.

Now, under Bernanke, it was like: have a press conference, have a statement, have the dots, be out there, give speeches, etc.

We're not going to get all the way back to the radio-silent days that I remember. But we are going to move in that direction. So there's going to be a lot less information coming out of the Fed. And Warsh hates forward projections because he knows they're wrong. He doesn't like the dots because he knows they're wrong. Why keep talking if you're making it up?

下一次会议的预测

What is policy going to be? My expectation for the meeting coming up next week is they're going to leave rates unchanged.

  • Case for raising rates: all the inflation we talked about that is coming.
  • Case for cutting rates: unemployment going up and the economy maybe going into a recession.

There's no reciprocity or inverse correlation between rates and unemployment — or inflation and unemployment, I should say. They can both go up, and they are. When that happens, you got to pick one because you can't fight them both at the same time.

For right now, there's a large group on the FOMC that absolutely wants to raise rates — probably 4 or 5 members. There's a smaller group who think you should cut rates because we're heading for a recession — probably 2 or 3 members. And there's a group in the middle. So I think they're going to compromise and just do nothing.

鲍威尔的"钉子"

And remember, Jay Powell is still on the board. Kevin — he's out as chair and Kevin Warsh is the new chair. But typically, because your term as chair is 4 years but your term as a governor is 14 years, and Powell is out as the chairman but he's still on the Board of Governors, and he will be till 2028.

When was the last time a chair stepped down and did not resign from the Board of Governors, stayed on the Board of Governors? 1949, Marriner Eccles. So it's been almost 80 years since this happened.

But Powell's doing it just to poke a stick in Trump's eye. Because if Powell leaves as a governor — which everyone has done, like I say, for 80 years — that would create a vacancy and Trump could appoint somebody, and Powell doesn't want to give Trump that degree of freedom.

So Powell said it. Imagine you're Kevin Warsh and you're coming in, you're chair of the meeting, you're in the boardroom — I've been in the Fed boardroom — and Jay Powell is sitting right next to you like, "Okay, he's not the chair, but he's got friends and he's kind of looking over your shoulder." So it's a tough spot.

I expect them to do nothing for now, but I do expect inflation to go up as we described.

AI 泡沫：3,600 亿美元的循环融资

Alex: Now I want to shift to another topic which we also mentioned last time, which is the AI topic. You've also written about this — industry publishers highlighting a roughly $236 billion of AI-linked debt issuance in 5 months. Where exactly is the dangerous mismatch? Is it in the debt maturity, the utilization, the customer credit power, the lag before revenue covers the capex? Where do you see it go wrong?

Jim: All of the above.

代币化商业模式的问题

It hasn't shown any revenue potential. What the hyperscalers and the AI frontier model creators — such as OpenAI, Anthropic, a few others — are doing is they're taking their large language model processing capability and their AI applications and they're tokenizing it. It's like buying a bus ticket. As a user, you can buy a certain number of tokens, which is basically processing power in these applications, and then use them for whatever application you want in your industrial process or service process — hospital, bank, could be anything.

And what they're finding is that AI — is it powerful? Yeah. Can it add some productivity? Yeah. But not that much. It's nowhere near enough to justify the expense.

So people are looking at the tokens and saying, "I'm not going to pay this price for these tokens because I'm not getting that much productivity out of it." Now if you lower the price down here, okay, I'll use some. It has some value. But if you put the price down here, the vendor can't pay the debt.

循环融资的把戏

So much of this is circular financing: - Chip producers like Nvidia are investing in end users like OpenAI and Anthropic and Google. - Those users are investing in Oracle and Nvidia and Amazon Web Services and other service providers.

The point is they're all investing in each other to prop the whole thing up. But the outside investor interest has not been that great.

The end users are like, "Lower the price and talk to me, but the price is too high." So it's not going to live up to the hype.

I'm not saying it's not useful, and I'm not saying it's not going to be around. It is powerful and it's here to stay. I'll grant that. And it can add to productivity. I'll grant that. But not that much.

"泥浆循环"：AI 的工程灾难

The confusion, the hallucinations, the unreliability, the slop — the fact that the AI models, the GPT models, train on the internet. But you need a — if you have a large language model, okay, what language are you looking at with your large language model? Well, they're looking at the internet — a billion, billion pages or whatever.

But what's happening is that as these models are being applied, they're producing output. The output is going into the internet. The output is flawed. They call it slop. So you're basically polluting the pond. The internet is filling up with slop. So you come back for more training and you're getting more slop in the outputs.

By the way, this is not just a metaphor. There are very regular scientific papers — I read a number of them — that say that's exactly what's happening. It's an engineering disaster.

It's not going to live up to the hype. The revenue models don't work, and it's all going to come crashing down. It doesn't mean the end of AI. What it means is that some of these firms are going to fail. A lot of this debt is going to go into default, and you're going to see a major bubble pop.

The problem with bubbles is people say they're hard to spot, which is not true. They're easy to spot. What's hard is to know when they're going to pop, and that is difficult. They can go on for a long time, but we're certainly getting closer to the end.

分析财报的正确视角：现金不撒谎

Alex: What would you be looking at more precisely? Is it the earnings report at the end of the month from all the major companies? I think Alphabet is having reports by the end of the close today, Meta next week, Microsoft as well. What exactly are you looking at in terms of numbers or the balance sheets?

Jim: Well, I think the balance sheets are actually more important. The problem with the revenues and all that — it's just a game. They beat expectations, and then Joe Kernen on CNBC says, "You beat expectations!" But they've set the expectations in a place they know they're going to beat them. It's just a big game.

The difficulty is those are all huge companies and they have a lot of other businesses, and some of the other businesses are very good. I mean, they're basically advertising agencies. So the advertising revenue and the social media revenue could be fairly strong even as the AI revenue is a disaster, but they don't break it out — not to that level of specificity. So some good businesses are going to mask the weakness in the AI.

Meanwhile, you've got pure AI plays that are trying to do IPOs — like OpenAI, Anthropic, and other companies that are more pure AI like Palantir and others. I'm not saying they're bad companies. I'm just saying they're not going to live up to the hype.

I don't really take very much from the income statement because there's a lot there and they don't break out the level of detail you need to really figure out the AI. You need insiders to basically explain it.

But the balance sheet is interesting because all this debt is piling up on the balance sheet.

And look at cash. I do a lot of balance sheet analysis. First thing I look at is cash — because cash doesn't lie. If you've got goodwill or accounts receivable or other intangibles, fine — I just write those off. Show me the money. But cash doesn't lie. And if you have negative — and also the cash flow statement and the balance sheet — if your cash is dwindling, your cash flow is negative, your debt's going up, you're heading for a train wreck. I don't care what your earnings are.

白银：两个矢量的双重驱动

Alex: One last topic if you have still time to answer one question, Jim.

Jim: Yeah.

Alex: Is silver. We haven't talked about silver in this conversation. It dropped more than 50% even though obviously it had wild moves right before that. And it also has some tie into everything we should said before — military defense, energy, AI servers. We need silver to also build those hyperscalers and servers. So what is your concluding note regarding silver?

Jim: Yeah, silver is — for the reason you mentioned, Alex — silver is more difficult to analyze than gold because it's — I mean, gold's not good for anything except money. I think it's the best form of money, your store of wealth. Gold is the best, but it's not used for much else. They coat space helmets with it, and some 5-9's wiring — but I've been in all the big refineries and talked to the top people about it. That's pretty scarce. Gold is incredibly valuable as a store.

Well, silver has a lot of industrial applications, and you mentioned some of them — electronics, catalytic converters, and other inputs — and it's a precious metal. So you've got two vectors. They can both be going up or down, or one can be going up when the other one's down. So you have to take that into account.

But I would say both vectors are pointing higher: - Industrial vector: going to give silver a boost because there's so much more defense spending and electronic spending. We're talking about hardware, not AI software — missiles and cruise missiles, hypersonic missiles, anti-missile missiles, and a lot of other applications, and drones — which the US is ramping up, but so is Europe (Germany's talking about it). So that input will remain strong. - Precious metals vector: silver is along for the ride. It tends to lag gold, but if gold goes up the way I expect, and I think it will, then silver is going to be along for the ride.

So silver will do fine.

中国黄金战略：透明与非透明的两本账

Alex: Thank you, Jim. Do you maybe have one last comment about China's policies regarding gold ownership, or do you want to just run it off now?

Jim: China's policies on what? I'm sorry.

Alex: Gold ownership. They just recently forbid any kind of leverage trading, and they're also inciting gold accumulation. And we've maybe also talked about this in the past — the fact that China has been accumulating consistently for many decades and surpassing much more the few thousand tons of gold that they actually reported to have. Some estimates like Alasdair Macleod say they have about 30,000 tons of gold, hinting towards like they might be preparing a UN-backed gold system in one way or another.

Jim: Yeah. As far as China and gold is concerned, China is accumulating a lot of gold, has been for a long time.

Their reported reserves from the People's Bank of China — and again I'll go back to 2009, because that's a good baseline — was 600 metric tons. Today it's closer to 3,000 metric tons. But there's every reason to believe that they have at least double that, possibly more.

They have another entity called the State Administration for Foreign Exchange (SAFE), which is a sovereign wealth fund, but it's off the books. It's non-transparent. So the People's Bank of China is transparent, but that's only where some of the gold is. A lot of the gold is in SAFE, and that's non-transparent. We don't know exactly how much is there, but every reason to believe that there could be 3,000 or 4,000 tons perhaps, or more. That would put China ahead of the United States in terms of total gold reserves.

They are moving to diminish the role of futures markets or paper gold or leverage gold trading, and move to physical gold trading — make Shanghai a center. It's very, very far down that road already.

关于 Macleod 的 30,000 吨估算

As far as third-party estimates — I was doing my — about 30,000 tons: I don't know where he gets that. You have to be careful when people throw numbers around like that.

If you're saying, "Let's combine all the gold owned by the central bank and the State Administration for Foreign Exchange and all the gold owned by the people of China," it could be 20 to 25,000 metric tons. That wouldn't surprise me.

But what's owned by the people is not the same as what's owned by the government. And I have this debate with friends in India. The Reserve Bank of India owns a little over 500 metric tons. I have a lot of friends in India. I was there last year, spent a lot of time there. And they go, "Oh no, Jim, we have 15,000 tons. Don't you know?" I said, "I know you have 15,000 tons, but it's all on Indian brides. It's all personal savings accounts. You wear gold chains because it's going to pay for your home or your kids' education or your retirement or healthcare or whatever."

So yes, there are 15,000 metric tons of gold in India, but only about 500 in the central bank. The rest is owned by the people.

So if Alasdair Macleod is saying that the people of China have that much gold — I've been to China a lot of times. I've been in gold boutiques. You go in, they have ladies in tight silk dresses walking around with gold on display, and they're open late, and people buy it. But that's not the same as central bank, which is what I really look at because that is going to have more impact on currency.

黄金支撑的人民币？"这是无稽之谈"

The gold-backed yuan is nonsense. That's not happening. They don't have enough gold for that. And they also don't have any of the other features that you need to run a reserve currency.

There's no such thing as reserve currency. They're only reserve assets. They are denominated in a currency, so that matters. But you don't have piles of cash in the basement of the central bank. What you have are US Treasury securities, or Bunds, or Italian government bonds, or maybe Japanese government bonds.

So you need reserve assets. To be a so-called reserve currency, you need a bond market. China doesn't have one. So they can't be a reserve asset. Clear.

结语与订阅信息

Alex: Thanks a lot, Jim. Well, to the explanation regarding Alasdair's calculation — he just laid it out in the videos, which I will not want to butcher now in a way that I can recall and paraphrase him in the wrong way.

But thanks a lot for your wealth of knowledge, time, Jim. Always appreciate talking to you. Do you have any comments or things that you want to give the listeners or viewers related to your newsletter or any other things?

Jim: Yeah, I publish a newsletter. It's called Strategic Intelligence. My publisher is Paradigm Press. It's easy to find — you can just Google "Paradigm Press Jim Rickards" or "Paradigm Press Strategic Intelligence". You'll find our landing page.

We put a lot into it — 12 monthly issues. I write all the lead articles; we have other contributors. All the kinds of ideas we've discussed on this podcast, they're all in that publication. We stay ahead of the curve.

And I'm on X — formerly Twitter, but X today — @RealJimRickards. So hope people join me there or subscribe to the newsletter.

Alex: Thank you, Jim.

大多数观察者把"油价没暴涨、供应链没断裂"当作 Rickards 预测失灵的证据。但这里藏着一个反直觉的系统性真相：**正是"表面平稳"消耗了系统最后的缓冲**。战略石油储备、化肥储备、氦气储备——这些都是"看不见的减震器"。当所有玩家（中国烧更多煤、美国增出口、俄罗斯补缺口、各国动储备）齐心协力"维持假象"时，他们并没有解决问题，而是**把弹簧压到了极限**。
这让我想起 2008 年金融危机前的"大缓和"（Great Moderation）——恰恰是"稳定"本身孕育了脆弱性。**Minsky 的金融不稳定假说在地缘政治层面复演了**：稳定期越长，参与者越倾向于消耗冗余，直到系统失去自我修复能力。当下我们看到的"没什么大事发生"，本质上是一场沉默的库存清算。

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] The Genocide That Gave China Its Borders – Sarah Paine
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被遗忘的准噶尔：地图上的"负空间"才是理解中国的钥匙

大多数人看中国地图，看到的是"有什么"——汉族聚居区、长城、黄河。但 Paine 让我们看到"没有什么"：准噶尔汗国从人类记忆中被彻底抹除了。这不是失败者写不了历史那么简单，而是连"存在过的证据"都被清算干净。

这里有一个反常识的观察：我们通常把"中华文明五千年绵延不断"视为一种温和的文化韧性，但从地形-气候-民族叠加图看，它其实是一种"生态位垄断"的暴力结果。汉族之所以占据了所有能种粮食的土地，不是因为他们更勤劳或文明更高，而是因为在垂直陡峭的地貌里，可耕地是零和资源——你活下来就意味着别人必须死或者逃。今日新疆的处境，不是"新政策"，而是这套两千年操作系统的又一次运行。

二、"选择性祖先认领"——中国如何用敌人的版图证明自己

Paine 抛出的最尖利的悖论：当代中国主张的"历史疆域"，恰恰来自元、清两个征服王朝——也就是汉人做亡国奴的时代。这在逻辑上等同于印度声称大英帝国的殖民地边界是自己的"神圣领土"，或墨西哥用阿兹特克帝国+西班牙殖民地叠加来划界。

这里藏着一个跨领域的连接：这种"祖先认领"的操作在企业并购史里有个对应物——公司被收购后，被收购方常常反过来把收购方的品牌资产、渠道、专利算作"我们家的传统"。汉文明是历史上最成功的"文化反向收购者"：军事上被征服，然后花两三百年把征服者的行政机器、疆域、乃至身份认同全部吞并消化，最后声称"这本来就是我们的"。蒙古人被赶回草原时，带不走他们征服的成果；满人到民国已经在户口本上消失。这是一种极其罕见的"输了战争，赢了叙事，最后连土地都收回"的三段式。

三、"军队以十万计"——被忽略的战争工业化时间差

Paine 一句轻描淡写的话值得反复咀嚼："中国动辄组织几十万人规模的军队已有数千年，而西方直到拿破仑战争才常规化做到这一点。"

这意味着中国比欧洲早了大约两千年进入"大规模社会动员"状态。我们习惯把工业革命当成现代性的起点，但从"组织能力"这个维度看，中华帝国其实是没有蒸汽机的工业化组织体——它用官僚系统、驿站、粮仓、户籍完成了欧洲需要铁路和电报才能做的事。

跨领域的意外连接：这或许能解释一个当代谜题——为什么中国互联网公司能把"996"、"大厂动员"、"人海战术"做到全球独一档。这不是文化性格，而是大规模人力协同的组织记忆残留。当字节跳动一年招几万人打一场产品仗时，它调用的是同一套两千年老代码。硅谷的"小而美工程师文化"在这套操作系统面前，更像是罗马军团遭遇蒙古骑兵——不是谁更聪明的问题，是组织尺度不在一个数量级。

真正令人不安的洞见：Paine 展示的地图告诉我们，中国的边界不是"谈判出来的"，而是"耕地能长到哪里、军队能杀到哪里"两条曲线的交集。如果我们相信气候变化正在重塑降水线和农业带，那么这张一千年稳定的"汉族核心-游牧边疆"结构图，可能正处于两千年来第一次真正的重绘前夜。而这一次，重绘的方向可能是向北——那意味着俄罗斯远东。

📝 转录文本

一、大陆帝国的地理底色

All right. Uh, whirlwind tour of China on what it looks like to be a continental empire.

So, here's a precipitation map — here's where it doesn't rain very much. Here's temperatures — that's where it's awfully cold. Here's topography — that's where it's flat.

So, if you notice, you want to grow things, you need it where it's warm enough, it rains enough, et cetera. And here's a really good topographical map. And it gives you an understanding of why famine afflicted China for so many centuries of its history, and why it's dependent on food imports today. It's just too much of the real estate's vertical to grow things on.

二、民族地图与"最好的地"的归属

And then, here's an ethnic map. You can see the consolidated pink area — that's where the Han, the preponderant ethnic group of China, live. And then they're surrounded with all these heterogeneous areas around them. You can go, "Hmm, I wonder what's going on there."

And then, here is a simplified ethnic map. It shows China proper. And the curious might ask, "How did the Han wind up with all the prime real estate?" Cuz what's arable is there.

And the answer would be: well, they laid waste to the competing Dzungar and Tibetan empires. I bet you've never heard of the Dzungars. They were wiped out by the Qing Dynasty a long time ago.

And in the continental world, you're faced with a binary choice — you either become Han, or they will kill you. And so, you got to get out of dodge and flee south, or do something else. And genocide is what happens to the losers in continental warfare. And apparently, in our own day, the Uyghurs are slated for genocide.

三、王朝快进：扩张、收缩与征服

All right. I'm going to give you a whirlwind tour, sanitized version of Chinese history.

The Han start up up north in the Yellow River Valley, and they spread, and they spread, and they do fun stuff like they build walls, and they build more walls — not a new idea. And then, they shrink back. And oh, that bad bad time. But then, they're back. And then, I don't know what happened there. But anyway, they're — they're — oh, consolidated.

And then, there's this thing which looks like any other Dynasty except a little bigger. Uh, not so — the Yuan Dynasty are Mongols. They're not Han. This is an occupation Dynasty, and that map's inaccurate. Cuz here's the real story: the Mongols start out east of Lake Baikal, and then they spread in concentric rings more or less over the Eurasian plain in another time of climate change, when their herds — they just had to move south or everyone's going to freeze to death.

The Chinese act like it's like any other Dynasty. No, it's not. It's the Pax Mongolica. It's the Mongol uh world order, when the Han were subjugated people. But they come back with the Ming Dynasty.

But then the Ming succumb to the second largest empire in Chinese history, another conquest Dynasty. These folks aren't Han. They're Manchu.

四、"选择性祖先"的悖论

And what's fascinating is today, when China claims whatever it's historical lands are, they either choose the Mongol Yuan Dynasty or the Manchu Qing Dynasty — when the Han were subjugated people. So try to un— untangle that logic. I'm not even going to go there.

Um, but the point was not to make that snide remark — although I did make that snide remark. Uh, but rather to show you that there's been lots and lots of expansion, lots and lots of shrinkage, and lots and lots of bloodshed while this is taking place.

五、被低估的组织尺度

China has been raising armies denominated in hundreds of thousands of people for thousands of years. The West does not do this — at least not on a regular basis — until the Napoleonic Wars.

Uh, it's a brutal world.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →
